speakeroldname: Mr. T. A. M. Kirk (Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thought probably hon. members would prefer it if I gave a more or less general report on the operations of the Post Office Department for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1955, before proceeding to a discussion of the estimates for the fiscal year 1955-56 which are now before the house for consideration.
The fiscal year which closed on March 31, 1955, was the largest in the history of the postal service from the standpoint of the volume of mail handled and revenue collected. The increase in the number of pieces handled during the year was approximately 6 per cent. This resulted in a total of approximately 3,355 million pieces. The revenue increased from $129 million to $151 million, which is approximately a 17 per cent increase.
It is estimated that on the 1954-55 year's operations there will be an apparent surplus of revenue over expenditures of approximately $5 million, but this does not take into account the rental on accommodation supplied by the Department of Public Works on the one hand, or the amount involved in free postage privileges on the other. The annual rentals on buildings provided by the public 
works department is estimated by that department at $13 million for the last fiscal year. The free postage privilege represents an amount which is estimated as being in the neighbourhood of $5 million.
During last year the department completed the reorganization of the postal service in accordance with the major recommendations made in the Woods-Gordon report. The benefits of this reorganization and the subsequent decentralization of authority to field officers are already being felt. There have been considerable improvements made in the service during the fiscal year, which have resulted in greater efficiency and increased economy.
As the human element enters to an appreciable extent into the operations of the postal service it is impossible to entirely eliminate irregularities due to individual errors, but the department is continually endeavouring wherever possible to take the necessary corrective measures. This is why we appreciate the cases which have been brought to our attention from time to time, which have enabled us to make inquiries and take remedial action when necessary.
Unfortunately many of the complaints made are based on incorrect information, and are often attributable to a non-observance by the complainants themselves of the regulations issued by the department for their guidance. It is largely for this reason that we request exhibits in the way of envelopes or wrappers when dealing with complaints. During the year there have been' numerous extensions of service. In the rural districts the number of rural mail routes has been increased by 56. In addition there have been 574 extensions granted, and the frequency of service has been increased in the case of 80 routes. As a result direct service has been given to more than 21,500 additional householders.
In regard to letter carrier delivery in the urban centres, in addition to the points where letter carrier delivery has been inaugurated there have been numerous extensions of existing routes, so that the total number of points of call made by letter carrier has increased by 93,500.
Group boxes have been installed both on rural routes and on the periphery of letter carrier delivery. This service is becoming increasingly popular and at the present time constitutes the method of delivery to more than 4,000 families, who in the majority of cases formerly had to go to the post office for their mail.
Since the amendment to the Post Office Act providing that the Postmaster General may

increase the rate of payment to mail contractors under certain conditions, more than 5,000 applications have been received. Upward adjustments have been effected in over 3,500 cases, and the actual additional expenditure through these adjustments is now approximately $850,000 per annum, which will be increased as additional cases are dealt with and adjustments granted.
Some 35 new motor vehicle services have been established. Some of these superseded rail services, in some cases due to the withdrawal of the trains, and generally the change has resulted in an improvement in the mail service.
The last fiscal year was the initial year of the five-day 40-hour week in the operating service. This resulted in an additional expenditure of approximately $4,600,000 and involved additional staff to the extent of 1,400 employees. The additional volume of mail handled and the improved service given have necessitated increases in staff, but these increases bear a very favourable comparison with the increase in the number of pieces handled and the increase in revenue.
The policy of the department is to reduce overtime wherever practical and this has been accomplished to a large extent by the employment of casual or part-time help. Overtime is, however, necessary, particularly at the Christmas period when the volume of mail increases manyfold, and also on statutory holidays.
There has been continued improvement in the letter carrier delivery service to those residential areas which receive one delivery a day, and although there were a number of complaints when the one delivery per day was established, these have been considerably reduced. The five-day week and delivery on six days a week involve a rotation problem which cannot be avoided, so that deliveries must be made periodically by relief carriers who are not so well versed on all the details of the routes as are the regular letter carriers.
As regards revenue postmasters, that is to say the postmasters who are in charge of the small offices, the department, after extensive study, is introducing a new system of payment. The annual rates of compensation which are already being paid in some instances and which will be paid in all cases in future will be based on the work load of the office rather than the actual revenue. This will be a much fairer system in so far as the individual postmasters are concerned, as in a number of cases the revenue did not properly reflect the work of the office.
The employment conditions of revenue postmasters are further being improved
Supply-Post Office
under the terms of the Public Service Superannuation Act. It is estimated that 1,200 additional postmasters will now fall within the provisions of that act. This is a privilege which is greatly appreciated by these hard-working postal employees. Further, 28 offices have been raised from a revenue to a semi-staff basis. This means that the postmasters and staffs of these offices are now paid according to a classified fixed salary wage, and receive benefits comparable to those enjoyed by civil servants. In addition 22 semi-staff post offices have been reclassified to full staff basis, which means that employees in those offices will have the full status of civil servants.
One of the features which has an important bearing on the public service is that of postal accommodation. Unfortunately at the present time our accommodation is inadequate in many centres. This is due to two main factors, namely the continued appreciable growth of the postal service, and the fact that during wartime and in the period subsequent thereto the building program was somewhat retarded.
During 1954-55 some 35 projects of different sizes were completed which will facilitate service to the public. There are in addition 61 projects which are either under construction or for which tenders have been called. These include such large buildings as the post offices at Vancouver, Winnipeg, Regina, and other comparatively large centres. Furthermore, there are 131 projects for which plans are being prepared and studied further, both by the public works and post office departments.
The department is continuing to study and develop the most economical and efficient method of mail handling. We have also initiated a program of work simplification. Significant progress is being made along these lines which we feel will further improve the efficiency of the service. The department is pioneering and developing a system of electronic sortation, and is also developing mechanical facing-up machines which will not only speed up the handling of the mail but will render the performance of post office tasks performed by the individual employees less onerous and laborious.
The number of employees in the postal service, including mail contractors, now totals approximately 50,000. Of these approximately 23,000 are civil servants, 13,000 are mail contractors and the balance, approximately 14,000, are the postmasters and assistants in revenue post offices.
There has been a continuous development in the transportation of mail by air. In the domestic service, the increase in the weight limit of "all-up" letter mail to eight ounces

Supply-Post Office
has resulted in a sharp increase in the volume carried, with corresponding advantages to the mailing public. In the international sphere the department has extended its services wherever air transportation is available, and has developed air transportation to many international points for parcel post and other categories of mail in addition to letters.
A reduction in international air transportation charges has enabled the department to reduce postage rates to the mailing public, and also to extend the 10-cent air letter form to any post office in the world.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with the acting minister in hoping for, in the name of all members of the official opposition, the early return of the Postmaster General. At the same time I would express our congratulations to the parliamentary assistant who is acting for him in the presentation of his estimates.
The parliamentary assistant has painted a rosy picture of the activities of the department, but I must say the Canadian public certainly had the right to hear of great improvements in the Post Office Department, especially since this year the estimated revenue of the department-that is for the fiscal year 1954-55-will be $132 million, which means $22 million more than last year, while the expenditures will show an increase of $13 million.
I would imagine that with this increase of $13 million in expenditures the department must have made great improvements all across Canada. The situation must be very different from what it has been in previous years. During the discussion of the present estimates I hope the parliamentary assistant will have the opportunity of giving us many examples of these improvements. There is, however, one place where I believe improvements are greatly needed. I refer to the problems of the suburban areas of our great cities across Canada.
By its policy the Post Office Department, in previous years, has caused a great deal of hardship to the people who are settling in the suburban areas around these big cities. In practically every new housing development in Canada the post office was always the last service to be offered to the people. Most of the time the municipal authorities were spending hundreds of thousands of dollars-even a million dollars-to provide the new suburbs with water, sewage and streets. The school boards were spending money. The telephone companies and power companies were trying to help these people. Usually the only thing missing was the postal service.

The postal service is always given about a year or two after these people have been established. Most of the time they were obliged to practically form an association and then enrol the support of the chamber of commerce, the municipal council and the churches in order to get even a mail box. I remember a few cases of that kind. Then they had to work for years following the same routine and making appeals to their members to get a certain service. Most of the time their campaign to get postal service was blocked by some sort of semi-secret regulation in which there was always some clause that prevented any improvement. There was always some regulation standing in the way; the houses were too far apart, they were so many yards apart or there were not enough houses on the street, and so on and so forth.
After the municipalities and the school boards had spent millions of dollars, it is hard to imagine that the Post Office Department would not believe in spending $25 for a mail box or a half hour or an hour of the mail carrier's time just to give these people some service. It sounds ridiculous, but I have witnessed some real hardship in my own riding.
I remember that in Three Rivers we had such a new district where most of the men were labouring men who worked until six o'clock at night in an iron foundry. It was then too late for them to go to the post office, which was at least two miles away from their houses. They therefore were obliged to send their children there after school, either by bicycle or bus, just to get, most of the time, a bill or some advertisement by mail. That situation lasted for more than two years. Improvement was always blocked by some regulation saying that between two houses there was a distance of over 80 yards. Finally after many representations the situation was corrected, but it took a long time. For these people the situation was really discouraging. I therefore hope that with the great surplus the department has this year- I mean now that the department is rich- we shall have some definite planning to look after these special cases.
Speaking about special cases, may I say that we have one in my riding, and it is a fair illustration of what these regulations of the postal department are like. In my riding we have an island called Wayagamack island, where we have one of the biggest paper mills in Canada. We have about 25 families living on this island, which is connected with the city of Three Rivers by a bridge. It is, in fact, within the city limits of Three Rivers. The people on that island have had

mail service since 1917. They had that mail service until January 31, 1951, when the collapse of the bridge across the St. Maurice river stopped the mail for a while. On August 13, about eight months afterwards, the communications were repaired and the service was re-established, so everything was all right. This service these people had enjoyed for over 30 years was re-established. But unfortunately the postal department discovered there was a certain regulation they could apply, and they cancelled the service.
Ever since then these people have been trying to get their postal service re-established. They tried to get it by means of all kinds of requests. They sent requests and even delegations to the deputy postmaster general, but to no avail. After having had the service for 30 years, we now find that the postal department have decided these people are not entitled to it. If the department felt for 30 years that these people deserved the service I think it sounds rather silly all of a sudden to invoke some regulation in order to stop such a service.
Now that the department has a great deal of money on hand, or has a great surplus, I think it is about time something was done. I suggest that at the next session of parliament a committee of the house should be set up to study these regulations. So far as I know the regulations are not codified. I think it is time the government set up such a committee, in which people with experience from all across Canada could sit around a table and discuss these regulations. I am quite sure there are some regulations that must be absolutely out of date and of such a nature that they do not fit into the regular life of our Canadian people.
For instance, there are certain regulations which state that in order to get a post office, a town must have so many people; that in order to have delivery of mail in certain areas by carriers there must be a certain population, and so forth.	These regulations
worked very well for a while, but I think it is about time they were reviewed. I believe this would be a grand opportunity for the government to set up a committee to discuss these matters. Most members have had a good deal of experience with these things, and cases are different from one end of Canada to the other.
I know, for instance, that in the city of La Tuque, north of Three Rivers, delivery by mail carrier has been an electoral promise for the last 30 years. It sounds a bit strange that a city of the importance of La Tuque cannot get service by mail carrier. I know there is always some regulation in the postal department which says that for such and
Supply-Post Office
such a reason these services cannot be provided, but I think all these regulations should be reviewed. Now that the department has enough money to make some real improvements, this is the proper time to correct the situation and remove the hardship from the people of these cities.
There is another point I should like to raise, having to do with a situation that I think is not quite fair. It has to do with the cost of mailing letters between Cap de la Madeleine and Three Rivers. The two cities are adjacent to each other, and are only separated by the St. Maurice river. Many of the people of Cap de la Madeleine work and do their business in Three Rivers, and the reverse is also the case to some extent. It is rather surprising that the people there have to pay an extra cent to send mail from Cap de la Madeleine to Three Rivers and vice versa, when on the island of Montreal a letter can be sent a distance of 10 or 15 miles at exactly the same rate of postage.
I think these matters should be discussed and corrected. I believe it would also be good for the people of Canada if the regulations were codified so that every time a special situation arose in some part of Canada the people of the area would be able to look at the regulations and see what they had to do to get mail delivery. Up to now the practice has been that they have to write the deputy postmaster general, who issues a certain regulation to the local postmaster. I do not think this is the proper channel to have to go through. I believe the regulations should be set forth in codified form so that people all across Canada can go to the book and find out exactly what is what so far as mail service is concerned.
I was very pleased to hear the parliamentary assistant refer to a few improvements in the postal service, but I can assure him that the people of Canada, who had to suffer a tremendous increase in the rates of postage last year, should receive much better service than they used to get and are getting now.
The reduction in service from two deliveries to one delivery a day has hurt a lot of people. I know that on a certain street in my riding there is a man who is a great reader of the morning newspaper, Montreal Matin, and the poor man does not get his paper until around six o'clock at night. He is very disappointed. I think something should be done to rectify these special situations. Before we are finished with these estimates I hope the parliamentary assistant will be able to tell the house what great plans the Post Office Department has for the coming year,

Supply-Post Office
and will be in a position to announce to the house and the people of Canada great improvements in the postal department in the near future, because the department costs the people of Canada a lot of money and had quite a surplus during the last year.

Mr. Chairman, the members of this group would also like to express their keen desire to see the early return to active duty of the Postmaster General, with his genial personality. I think I can honestly say that if there is any cabinet minister whose absence we feel keenly it is the most pleasant Postmaster General of Canada. We are looking forward to the day when he will be in his place again and able to resume his responsibilities. We were highly impressed a year ago, when he was under very severe fire from the opposition, with the able manner in which he held his own ground.
At this time I should also like to express the appreciation of this group to the many thousands of employees of the Post Office Department. It is one department of government, in my opinion, in which you can notice a pride of service that is not found in any other department. Perhaps it is because the Post Office Department is many years old that we find a situation where even the humblest of civil servants in the department takes an intense personal pride in his responsibilities and in the fact that he is rendering a worthwhile public service.
Contrary to the attitude just expressed, I believe that on the whole the service rendered by the Post Office Department to the people of Canada is excellent. We retain our right, of course, to criticize what we consider are shortcomings here and there. That is our responsibility. However, I think the average Canadian is very much impressed by the most efficient service the Post Office Department is rendering to the people.
At this time I should also like to express the appreciation, as I know many other individuals and organizations have done, of the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia for the setting up of a metropolitan postal area there. In our opinion this step was long overdue. The cities of Montreal and Toronto and the areas surrounding them have had this great privilege for a goodly number of years, and Vancouver, the third largest metropolitan area in Canada, had to put up a fight in order to gain recognition.
I should like to say to the acting minister that when he set up the metropolitan area we were pleased to have him endorse the principle enunciated by the Postmaster General just before his illness. We were most pleased to see that the Acting Postmaster General did
fMr Balcer.l
not desert the decisions of the Postmaster General in his absence. However, I should like to point out to him that there are many little isolated places within the metropolitan area which he omitted to include at the time. I sincerely believe it was only an oversight. However, there are places that to all intents and purposes are part of this lower mainland metropolitan area. I hope it will not be too long before places like Port Moody, Port Coquitlam, North and West Vancouver will be included.
While I am speaking about the local situation I should also like to put in a plea for the early establishment of sub-post office facilities for the people of East Burnaby. This was one of the things mentioned at the time the Postmaster General was still able to assume his responsibilities. He did assure us that serious consideration would be given to this matter. We feel that the people of East Burnaby should have some sub-post office facilities so they would not have to spend the time going to North Burnaby, South Burnaby or New Westminster if they want to do any post office business.
Last year I noticed what in my opinion amounted to almost an admission by the Post Office Department that it was one of the few remaining departments of government in which patronage was still tolerated. While it was not said this system was endorsed, one almost got that impression. I should like to make a plea that any sign of patronage be removed at a very early date, because I think the prestige of any department of the public service is to a certain extent dependent on the absence of patronage. In so far as civil service matters are concerned, I believe we are getting away from pork barrel politics, and I should like to see the last vestiges of it removed from the Post Office Department.
I hope the recently announced regulation concerning the deduction of holiday time as a punishment for tardiness is not being applied. I feel that if there are civil servants who repeatedly show up late for work, they should be dealt with as they would be in any other line of employment. The civil servant who insists on being tardy should no longer be retained by the civil service; that is the only honest way of dealing with tardiness. I feel that this business of taking away a man's holiday which he needs, whether he is a tardy civil servant or otherwise, is not to be commended. After an adequate warning the civil servant should be dismissed, rather than have his holidays taken from him.
In connection with the civil service I may say also that I hope the government will see its way clear to setting an example in the

matter of fair employment practices. Rather than granting the 40-hour week only to those postal employees who work in an area where the 40-hour week is prevalent, the department should grant the 40-hour week to all employees, irrespective of what industry in the area may be doing. I feel also that some attention might be given to what I sometimes feel is the rather rapid turnover in employees in the Post Office Department. There seem to be a great number of postal employees resigning and taking other jobs. I think there could well be reasons for this large number of resignations. I do not believe it speaks very well for the post office as an employer when they have to hire large numbers of new employees to replace the members of the civil service who have left.
I listened with a good deal of interest to the speech by the hon. member for Three Rivers. He was complaining about the same thing that many of us are complaining about, and asked for a change in the regulations covering suburban areas. I do not know what change in the regulations he would want, but so far as I can determine there is really no policy in the Post Office Department covering service to growing areas of Canada. There seems to be a tendency to feel that once the post office is established it must remain the centre of distribution regardless of what happens to the area involved. It is readily understandable that those who are operating such post offices would wish to retain this ever-expanding area of service under their personal direction.
I believe the department should have definite conditions-I know that is what the hon. member for Three Rivers meant-that must be complied with before new services can be rendered. We should be able to look at the policy and determine whether or not a section is entitled to door to door delivery; whether it is entitled to these little red mail boxes connected with the pick-up service, or whether it is entitled to postal facilities in the corner store. There should be a policy that would enable us to determine whether an area would be entitled to the erection of a sub-post office. We feel that the policy of the department in connection with these things is far too vague. It may well be that the wheel that creaks the loudest first gets the grease, or it may be that the community that has the most influence with the department is able to get attention first.
We of the lower mainland feel we should not have had to use many of the tactics we had to employ in order to get the 4-cent letter rate. We feel that there should have
Supply-Post Office
been a policy covering such matters. I would once again, as I did a year ago, appeal to the acting minister to reduce the first class letter rate. I feel it is an imposition on the people who really need the mail service of Canada to ask them to subsidize the advertising of commercial enterprises. I feel we could very easily lower the 5-cent first class letter rate to 4 cents and still make ends meet if we raise the second class mail rate. I believe you would make many postal employees happy if you imposed such an additional tariff on second class matter, because it would discourage the use of this medium for the promotion of Rinso soap and things of that sort.
I was in the New Westminster post office some months ago, and saw the arrival of monthly magazines. I would call the attention of the acting minister to a recent innovation of the daily newspapers. In my area one may receive a daily newspaper for $1.50 a month, I believe it is; and if one agrees for the period of a year to pay an additional 40 cents a month to the local carrier boy one is entitled to choose from a number of magazines which will be delivered by mail. We in New Westminster are not particularly keen about the magazine known as True Story. We regard it as that much trash, and we used to get only one mail bag of this magazine each month. However, since the introduction of this offer at 40 cents a month the New Westminster office receives a dozen mail bags filled with issues of this one magazine.	When one considers that the
number of magazines available was extensive, that the list was very long, one can imagine at once the additional burden placed on the post office by this innovation of the daily newspapers.
There may have been a time in Canadian history when second class mail required the advantage of a subsidy. There is a howl in certain sections of Canada when mention is made of subsidies for useful purposes, including the sale of our wheat overseas and the sale of Canadian foodstuffs to the people of Canada as well as to other people in other parts of the world. However, I have yet to hear many objections to this hidden subsidy to commercial firms in Canada. If these were essential and the most useful forms of advertising I might not feel so keenly in the matter, but I do not see a particle of difference between Oxydol and Rinso soaps, and I see no reason whatsoever why our faithful civil servants should have loaded on their backs week after week hundreds of pounds of this useless trash, particularly when they might be rendering a much more useful service to society.

Supply-Post Office
There is one more point I would like to raise, one which up to now I have not had a suitable opportunity to call to the attention of the Acting Postmaster General. I had written about it to the Postmaster General, assuming that in his absence mail would be placed on the desk of the Acting Postmaster General or, failing that, at least on the desk of the parliamentary assistant. Instead of that I received a reply from the deputy postmaster general enclosing confirmation of an earlier decision by a lesser official. I resented that, because I feel that when I as a member of parliament write a letter in which I call into question some of the activities of a department, I should receive something more than a reply from a member of the civil service. I feel that is not the customary procedure. No other department of government has ever treated me in this way.
This is what happened. While the postmaster at Port Moody was absent on his holidays there was removed from the post office, by an alleged theft, the sum of $500. The Post Office Department is now withholding $50 a month from the salary of the postmaster at Port Moody until the $500 is recovered. I am told that in many post offices, even in offices as large as that at Port Moody, the postmaster is held responsible for what happens in his absence, even when he is away on holidays. If this is so, then certainly we are not helping those people to take holidays. I do not think postmasters should be held financially liable for whatever may happen in their absence.
I hope the Acting Postmaster General will look into the situation. The postmaster in question is one of the most highly honoured in the community.
Did I understand the hon. member to say that he had written me a letter to which I had not replied?

No, I wrote to the Postmaster General. However, I had assumed the letter would be placed on the desk of the Acting Postmaster General, or at least on that of the parliamentary assistant. I regret that for various reasons I was not able to call it to the attention of the Acting Postmaster General. I mention this merely to emphasize to him the way many members of parliament feel in regard to the Post Office Department; that there is a self-styled postmaster general of Canada who has no right to be a postmaster general because he has not been designated as such. In saying this I am referring to the deputy postmaster general.
I feel that the procedure of making the postmaster at Port Moody pay for something that happened in the post office in his absence is most unwarranted. This man is most highly

regarded in his home town. He is a veteran of the first world war. On two separate occasions, at great risk to his own personal safety, in cases of fires in that town he saved for the Post Office Department thousands of dollars. He has been an alderman for many years; and to have him thus penalized for something he had nothing to do with is not, in my opinion, a fair procedure when dealing with a good and faithful civil servant.
Then I have one other complaint, which I think is nation-wide. This complaint deals with the renting of post office buildings. I do not think we can argue that the government of Canada ought to own all the many small buildings in which post offices are housed. I do not think anyone would be logical in asking for that. I notice from the public accounts that in the year ending March 31, 1954 no less than 1,946 public buildings were rented by the government of Canada, through the Department of Public Works, where the rental was less than $250 a month. I assume that most of these buildings housed post offices. The total rental paid in that fiscal year for these buildings was $1,432,442.
I do not think one could argue against that expenditure. Indeed, on the whole we have expressed our satisfaction with it. A man who lives in a building and permits the government to use part of it as a post office is certainly entitled to receive some compensation. It would be poor business for the department to go out on a limb to the extent of erecting public buildings in every little hamlet in Canada.
However, the Department of Public Works, again chiefly on behalf of the Post Office Department, paid out in rentals in that same year the sum of $3,399,051. This was paid to people who received rentals for buildings in excess of $3,000 a year. In looking over the rates of rental paid I noticed that in one case it went as high as $2.20 a square foot a year. This is an exceedingly high rate for some of the smaller centres of Canada. In most of the urban centres of Canada adequate facilities might well be rented for $1 a square foot a year. That is considered a fairly high rate of return. I am just wondering why in some cases rentals are so high.
This is what I do not like to see happen, Mr. Chairman. Somebody is offered a lease by the Post Office Department, which agrees to rent a certain specified building for a 10-year period at a fixed yearly rental. This individual, who possibly does not even own a lot, much less a building, can then take the lease and walk over to see his bank manager and say, "I have an agreement with the government of Canada which will pay me for this accommodation so many dollars a month

for the next 10 years. I am willing to assign my rent to you. Will you lend me the money to buy the lot and put up a building?"
If we are not careful, Mr. Chairman, this is what can happen. A man can rent a building costing $25,000 for $500 a month. He is assured of paying the cost of the building through monthly payments of $250 without investing any money of his own whatsoever. He can receive a net return of $250 a month, yet make no contribution whatsoever to the public interest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit an interruption at this time? The Post Office Department does not rent buildings; it obtains them through the Department of Public Works. We tell them of our needs.

I fully realize that, Mr. Chairman. At the same time I also realize that the Department of Public Works will not put up a building for the Post Office Department unless the Post Office Department asks for a certain building to be put up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
We
ask for appropriate accommodation. We do not ask them to put up a certain building in a certain place. We want a building in a suitable location which will meet our requirements.

I am glad to have the parliamentary assistant now put the blame for what is happening on the Department of Public Works. If that is the case we shall raise the matter again when the estimates of the Minister of Public Works are before us. If that is the proper time to raise it, we certainly shall do so. However, if it is good business for an individual to put up a building in such heavily populated areas as the city of New Westminster, the municipal district of Burnaby, the city of Port Moody, the area around Surrey-and I know it is happening in other parts of Canada.-if it is in someone's selfish interests to put up a new building and lease it to the government of Canada, it is also good business for the government of Canada to own such public buildings and collect its own rents. If it were not profitable for those individuals to put up those buildings they would not do it.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary assistant has twice raised the point that this is not a matter for the Post Office Department; it is no concern of ours. Surely the hon. member would not mind saving it until the minister who is responsible has his estimates before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I shall end this discussion now. However, I am not fully
Supply-Post Office
satisfied that the Post Office Department is not in great measure responsible for obtaining certain accommodation from the Department of Public Works. I am not satisfied that it does not exercise some influence on whether or not public buildings are to be erected and owned by the government of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group are pleased to associate ourselves with the remarks that were made earlier in regard to the improvement in health of the Postmaster General and his return here in the very near future. We are looking forward to the day when he can return to his seat in the house next to the Acting Postmaster General.
I should like to compliment the parliamentary assistant on the very capable and efficient way he presented his report on the doings of the department in the past year.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned the new postal regulations having to do with the metropolitan area of New Westminster and Vancouver, under which my constituents come. I should like to associate myself with his commendable remarks in that respect. I want to compliment the government representative on the fine way in which the meeting was conducted. We possibly set a precedent, in that for the first time we had members of the Social Credit party, the C.C.F. party and the Liberal party in one room discussing a problem on which we reached an agreeable solution. However, it did call for some help from the people of Burnaby, who took it upon themselves to conduct a plebiscite and help the matter along. We in the area are very happy that such changes were made. The people in the north part of Surrey, which is now to be known as the North Surrey postal area, are very happy about the situation.
However, I am not on my feet for the purpose of extending only complimentary remarks. I am very happy to have the privilege of doing that and to pass them on, but for that reason I feel the department should know something else. In the course of his review the parliamentary assistant did indicate that the department was anxious to receive any information as to complaints, suggestions or recommendations the people had to offer, and would give them some consideration.
During the time I was at home at Easter, and earlier, I had occasion to meet with the letter carriers, the rural route carriers and the mail contract carriers, and discuss with them some of the problems with which they are faced. It might be possible to deal with some of the problems in a regulatory way.

Supply-Post Office
Others are problems that are common to the nation as a whole and should be made known here.
With respect to the contracts of the rural mail carriers, I find that the population of the area in which I live is growing rapidly. The Postmaster General and his parliamentary assistant are aware of that. That also applies to the departmental officials. There are some 15 rural routes which terminate in the postal district of New Westminster. Because of the increase in population in that area and the contracts having been let at an earlier time, we of that area find that while the mileage remains the same the number of stops is continuing to mount. It would be very interesting indeed to discover what discrepancy, if any, exists between the rates paid to United States rural route carriers, the prairie rural route carriers, the rural route carriers of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, and those in the mountainous area of British Columbia, including the lower mainland.
Another matter that bothers them considerably is the question of overtime and extra help. The report by the parliamentary assistant indicated that his department is cutting down on the amount of help that was supplied. These rural mail carriers are unhappy about that, as they feel they are being penalized. It is true that for a long time changes have not been made in respect of the regulations. From December 12 to December 31 the mail is particularly heavy when everyone is getting parcels or more mail than usual. These men have to do their own sorting, and are not given additional help.
1 know under our system of mail contracts it will be said they should realize that when they put in their bid. That probably is an answer that could be made. I shall deal with that point shortly. It is found that during the week these rural mail carriers work as much as 16 hours a day, as well as eight hours on Sunday, in order to get out the mail as efficiently as our post office officials have the right to expect them to do. They work also on statutory holidays such as May 24 and December 25. It is most unfortunate that of all the people in the nation only parliamentarians and rural mail carriers have to work on a holiday such as May 24. If these days are permitted as holidays for the ordinary civil servant we should go a step further and grant the same privilege to these 13,000-odd mail carriers.
Usually when a route is put up for tender there are about 350 boxholders on the list, but quite often within a very short time the

number of boxholders may increase to as many as 900, as has happened in my own area. Many of these men when bidding on these routes do not appreciate the potential growth, and they are afraid to bid high for fear they will not get the contract. It may be said that as they have contracted for the route they should go ahead and suffer the consequences, but I do not think the Canadian taxpayers expect these men to make deliveries to 500, 600, 720 or 802 boxholders when they have contracted to make deliveries to only 350. I do not think the public feel they should have to do that at the original contract rate.
This contracting system is actually unjust, for the reason I have just outlined. It is an antiquated system. It is something like the old tax collector who tendered for his job of collecting taxes. It is true that the mail carrier does not bring in revenue, but in order to obtain the contract he must underbid others for that particular job. Quite often the results are not the best, and poor service is given to the public.
I know the department was familiar with conditions on one rural mail route two or three years ago. In this case a particular individual had underbid for the route, and he obtained the contract. For four or five days after he took over the route people failed to get their mail, or it was misdirected. It was found the man could not read or write properly. More efficient men had bid on that route but were unable to get the contract. I must congratulate the postmaster at New Westminster for taking an active part in this matter and seeing that this man was replaced. But in the meanwhile there was this misdirection of mail, which would not have occurred had the proper man obtained the contract.
Oftentimes a route is changed and tenders must be called again. The experienced man knows the difficulties that will be encountered, but when he puts in a reasonable bid quite often he is underbid by someone who may have supplementary income, or who has little knowledge of how the mail should be carried and what work is involved. Yet that man gets the contract and we lose the benefit of the experience which the other man has to offer.
I have one case in mind in which a man was not given a contract in the beginning, but later on he replaced a most inefficient man, the one I spoke of earlier. This man had been with the department for a matter of 18 years.
Who is "we"? The hon. member says "we", and I should like to know it he is referring to the department.

I am referring to the people in the area to whom this man delivers mail. I happen to be one of those in the area and the "we" would include the people in the area. I think this is a matter that should be taken into consideration. We should consider the experience possessed by some of these men, and should take into account the lesser efficiency of a man who may underbid on a contract in order to get a particular route.
It may be true that the lowest tender is not always accepted. Frequently these men are brought into the district office and their bids are discussed, in the hope that they will bring them down to the lowest bid. The department is desirous of hiring the efficient and experienced carrier. I must say it has been found quite frequently that the department has been asked by some of these inexperienced people who have taken contracts that they be given increases, and quite frequently they get the increases from the department. The department realizes that their original bid was too low. But the result of all this is that the person with the greater knowledge of the route and who could have given the most efficient service does not get the job. Someone else gets the job, and then the rate is brought up to that at which the other man tendered.
Frequently the stock answer to a request for an increase is that the department does not feel that an upward revision in pay is justified, but should the man so desire the department will on 90 days' notice open the route for tender and the man will be free to bid again. That is the stock answer that is given when many of these experienced route carriers make these requests. They want to bid whenever there is an increase in pay because of changes in the number of boxholders, rerouting, or for some other reason.
This is a most unfortunate situation, and I do not think we are treating these men properly. They do not have a 40-hour work week; they do not receive any superannuation; they are not under the sick leave provisions, and they are granted no annual holidays. They pay their running expenses, which average about $100 a month, and they do not get the same benefits as do the letter carriers. They tender on labour.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam mentioned one of the other problems with which letter carriers have found themselves faced, namely this matter of subsidized advertising carried through our mails. Incidentally, this same complaint applies to both the
Supply-Post Office
letter carriers and the rural route carriers. As the result of an active advertising campaign on the part of the newspapers, as was explained by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, there has been a tremendous increase in the number of magazines which the letter carriers and rural route men are asked to carry. Two years ago it was rather usual for the letter carrier to have only two days on which his mail was particularly heavy, by reason of the fact that he had to carry more magazines on those days than on any others. However, today he has a heavy day every day.
The hon. member mentioned True Love magazine, I believe. I have others I could add to that list. There is Popular Science. The New Westminster post office used to receive a bundle and a half. Today they get 20 bundles of Popular Science. As to Parents Magazine, two years ago they got two bags; now they get 10 bags. Reader's Digest and other magazines are received in proportionate numbers.
According to the statement of the parliamentary assistant the post office is losing money. It is true it showed a $5 million net profit, but he said it failed to pay $13 million in rents to the Department of Public Works. In other words on a business basis it lost $8 million last year. In effect we are subsidizing these magazines. Whether they are cheap or whether they are good is not the important factor. It is the advertising contained in them that is supposed to be paying these charges, and not necessarily the householder, whether or not he buys those magazines.
The service to these magazines and to the publishers of other periodicals is greater than that given to air mail or first class mail. That, of course, is a situation which should not exist. We find that the postman notifies each publisher of the old and the new address. He notifies the United States publisher once and the Canadian publisher twice. He does not get any pay for this extra clerical work.
That raises a question that was mentioned earlier in respect to docking them one day's holiday for each three hours or five hours-I forget which it is-of time they are late within the year. These clerks quite frequently spend anywhere from 15 to 30 minutes a day after hours or during their lunch hour in redirecting magazines. This Post Office Department gets nothing for that service, nor do the men. However, if they happen to be 15 minutes late for a matter of three days-I forget just what it is now-or three hours late in the year, they lose a full day. Yet they do not get paid anything extra, whether it is 15 or 30 minutes extra they have to spend. I do not think that is playing the game fairly.

Supply-Post Office
It is not unusual to see these letter carriers redirecting mail for 15 to 30 minutes of their own time. These misdirected magazines and periodicals are forwarded for 90 days, as is all first class mail; and then they are treated as first class mail and there is no extra charge to the magazine publisher. A letter carrier finds it impossible to get his regular work done in regular hours. As I said, he gets no credit for this extra time put in after hours or during his lunch hour. It does not matter actually on what part of his route he happens to be when lunch time comes. If he is two or three miles away from the post office he is given no credit for the time spent travelling back and forth to get his lunch, etc. I would not say that he should necessarily receive any extra time for travelling, but we should not penalize him, as we are doing according to this regulation that was posted as of April 1, in respect of one day lost for three hours that he may have lost through coming late during the year.
I return to the magazine question. At the present time the clerk notifies the Canadian publisher twice, and then he returns the magazine to the company. Some of these publishers never take notice of a change of address. On examination I have discovered that there are certain magazines such as Eagles magazine and Western Grocer, which the larger publishers find it more economical to send to the Post Office Department and then have the clerk spend his time returning it to the publisher, and it never does get to the man who has subscribed to it originally. He apparently does not bother to get his address changed properly. As to one particular magazine that was drawn to my attention, namely Motor Coach Conductors and Operators the same address was kept on that magazine for ten consecutive years. I am not so sure that it does not still come to the same post office.
Such a condition should not exist, under which we continue to charge our clerks one day holiday for being the equivalent of three hours late during the year, and at the same time give them nothing for redirecting this mail; especially on heavy magazine days, which is every day now. Fifteen to thirty minutes are given to the Canadian people of the time of these men who deliver the mail.
There are certain recommendations I would propose that might be instituted. One is that we as the parliament of this country should ask our magazine publishers to have their magazines labelled in a particular place. I do not know whether hon. members have taken the time to study the magazines at

all. If you do so, just ask yourselves what you would do if you were a clerk and received a magazine that had to be redirected, let us say, back to the publisher. Do you know where you would find the publisher's name? I venture to say that if you brought 50 magazines in here you would find the addresser's name in 50 different places. That is a situation that should not be tolerated. If we want to use people's time properly we should ask that the name of the periodical and its address should be properly placed, let us say, on the inside cover or on page 1 or page 2, or some uniform place. It would not take anything from the cover of the magazine which seems to be the important thing but it could help these letter carriers and others in the postal department. It would save them considerable time.
The location of the names of the individuals to whom the magazines are addressed is something that might also bear some uniformity. It is helping cost the taxpayers this $8 million deficit that we will actually have for the year. Because it is costing us actual cash I think the people of Canada would be quite within their rights in asking that if a certain magazine reached a particular volume, the company should set up its own delivery system. Carrier boys deliver magazine such as Liberty and other publications, and I see no reason why the post office should subsidize magazine delivery.
There is another difficulty that is encountered. If you go into any large post office you will find magazines of all kinds stacked there. One magazine is to be delivered on May 24, let us say, another on May 27 and another on May 29. In this way we are providing a warehouse for some of these publications. Householders expect their magazines to be delivered on a particular day, and the person who takes the brunt of the blame is none other than the letter carrier. We cannot blame the householder. He has a right to expect that the magazine should be in his hands on the first Monday of the third week in the month, or whatever day it may be. However, by reason of the fact that the mail may be particularly heavy a great burden is loaded upon the letter carrier, who is not being treated in the same way as the ordinary worker in our cities and towns.
There are instances of mail coming into the post office marked, "Do not open until Christmas", or with instructions not to deliver it before a certain date. The post office personnel are particularly careful to try to please the person sending the mail and the person who is to receive it, but at times such as the Christmas season, when the amount of mail is particularly heavy, no one should expect

mail to be kept in the post office for any length of time. However, in their co-operative way the post office personnel try to serve the public as efficiently and as well as they expect to be served. They provide this service at a very nominal charge, but I do not think they should be expected to do so.
I suggest that magazine publishers should be told that their magazines will not be held for delivery on a particular date once they arrive in the post office. Efficient operation is not only a matter of getting the mail to the post office but of dispatching it as quickly as possible, and it should be gotten rid of as quickly as possible.
Another problem that is of concern at particular times of the year has to do with heavy catalogue deliveries. To the best of my knowledge the catalogues have to be tied in bundles by the letter carrier on his own time. In the case of a city such as New Westminster the catalogues are shipped there by freight, and the freight rate of course is very low. Then they are delivered by letter carrier at the local rate of 18 cents each. I do not know where our business sense has gone. The letter carrier has to tie these catalogues into bundles on his own time. It is his own time because we do not pay him anything extra for it. Then he has to deliver them to householders some distance from the post office at a rai,e of 18 cents each. It is economically unsound. The catalogues come in burlap sacks, and then they are handled in the same way as magazines. They are stored until ready for release according to the wishes of the particular firms.
These catalogues are entirely advertising and nothing else. Why should the letter carriers be burdened with them? New Westminster post office is not a particularly large one. There are only about 100,000 householders who receive their mail through that office, but I find that the average shipment of catalogues to the office weighs some 34 tons As you can well understand, that represents a great number of catalogues.
In most of our major cities and towns you will find mail order offices. If a person wishes to place an order with Simpsons-Sears or the T. Eaton Company or any other mail order house he can go to the mail order office and give the attendant his order, rather than use the mail to send the order to the company. At these offices he can either pay for his order or, if he has a credit account, the matter can be looked after in another manner. Instead of all these catalogues being handled through the post office, as they are today, I suggest that the different mail order houses be instructed to use a card system. I understand that some now do so to a certain
Supply-Post Office
extent. They should be asked to use a card system wherever possible to notify their customers that the catalogues are available at the local mail order office. Otherwise the postal rate for carrying the catalogues should be increased. The present rate for the handling of these items is only 18 cents which is unreasonably low.
Another complaint has to do with overtime. This question has been discussed in the house from time to time, but I for one am not satisfied that it has been handled properly. I am satisfied that if the deputy postmaster general or any of his staff were to check the larger post offices they would find postal clerks and letter carriers working after hours readdressing mail. This does not happen once or twice a year but once or twice a week, or oftener, and each time it may take a matter of 15, 20 or 30 minutes. If a person in industry has to work 10 or 15 minutes overtime he is paid for half an hour, but that does not apply in the Post Office Department.
The postal clerks and letter carriers are told that if they want to put in overtime they must come in earlier the next morning. If a letter carrier is in the habit of coming to work at 6.30 a.m. he should anticipate when he is going to have a particularly heavy load of mail and arrive at 5.30 a.m. Then the postmaster will recognize that the man is there for an extra hour and will give him an hour's overtime. I do not know whether it is because we mistrust our civil servants who deliver the mail that we have this kind of thing, but in my opinion we should not expect people to spend their evenings doing extra work and not pay them for it in the same way that industry treats its workers.
Another ground these men have for complaint is the fact that the check-up time, so far as letter carrier routes are concerned, is usually during the month of July. As everyone knows, July is a vacation month, and only about 65 per cent of the householders on a route are receiving delivery of mail. In the months of April and October, for example, 70 per cent or more of the householders are receiving mail, but by taking the month of July it is found that the figure is 65 per cent. Magazine subscriptions usually lapse at that time of the year. Catalogues are not distributed then, with the result that the mail is considerably less than usual. In speaking of the various letter carrier routes, it just means that once the fall and winter months are here the chore becomes more difficult. It means these carriers have to cover 70 per cent or more of a route which was actually set up on the basis of 65 per cent.

Supply-Post Office
There is one other fact that was drawn to my attention, and that concerns the matter of carriers' garments. On April 5 of this year I had tabled a return of sessional paper No. 112-E concerning the type of garment being used and the suppliers thereof. Question No. 3 read:
Who were the five chief suppliers of (a) summer weight trousers; (b) winter weight trousers, during each of the past five years?
The answer was Master Craft Uniform Company, Registered, Quebec, for the years 1950 to 1953 and Maurice Pollack Limited, Quebec, for 1954 and 1955. I find that particularly interesting because the letter carriers complain that whereas formerly their uniforms lasted for two or three years, they are now very fortunate to have a uniform last for more than two or three months. I do not know if there is any relationship between the fact that letter carriers are being docked $20 per month for clothing and the fact that there is a new supplier. I am not in a position to say. If it is a matter of $20 per month, as I have been led to believe, then that totals to a $240 per year deduction. I am not prepared to say that is correct because I have not checked with the minister or any of the departmental officials, but I think it is $20 per month. If that is so, I would strongly urge that consideration be given to the fact the men feel they would be much better off buying their own uniforms and getting the $240 because the old uniforms lasted them for two or three years.
I am quite aware of the fact that the recommendations I have made are going to cost money. There is only one possible place from which this money can come. My suggestion is that the second and third class mail, which frequently receives the same treatment as first class mail, be handled on a sound economic basis. If it costs more money to handle third class or second class mail, then certainly we should expect those people who use the service to pay the extra cost of it. I am not interested in where they are going to get the money, but I dare say the natural and obvious place would be from the advertisers who use the mails and whom the people of Canada are subsidizing.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to have this opportunity of adding my voice to that of the preceding speakers to express by best wishes to the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) and to wish him a prompt return to good health. I am also happy to congratulate those who have ensured the proper operation of the department during his absence.

The city of Chicoutimi, county town of the area which I have the honour of representing in this house, by virtue of its population, of its geographic location and of the beauty of the surrounding district, has been aptly named "Queen of the north". It is an important industrial, commercial, religious and educational centre; a progressive and lively city. It is the pride of those who live in the kingdom of the Saguenay and evokes the admiration of visitors because of its location, of its sunshine, of the warm hospitality and dynamic enterprise of those who live there.
It might possibly be perfect from a town planner's point of view if it had fewer level crossings, if the Canadian National Railways station were a more adequate structure, if its harbour installations were improved and the surrounding area beautified, and finally if the public buildings necessary to the proper discharge of various departmental activities were to be built there.
All these are things which come under the jurisdiction'of the authorities in Ottawa and about which we should complain every time we have an opportunity to do so. I rise in this debate to protest against a lack of appropriate facilities, for the postal service more particularly, which is prejudicial to my fellow citizens.
I shall speak as briefly as possible and merely recall certain oral or written representations made in that connection during the past years.
One of our weeklies wrote as follows on May 8, 1952:
Chicoutimi-Following the request made by the Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Fournier replied that the federal government would do everything in its power to start work on the new central post office by this summer.
On March 16, 1953, the minister wrote me the following letter:
Dear Mr. Gagnon:
I acknowledge receipt of your letter of March 13 regarding the construction of a public building at Chicoutimi, P.Q.
Any delay in the construction of that building is due to the fact that we do not know definitely which departments will occupy it nor what floor area will be required by each of them.
Yours very sincerely.
On April 9, 1953, I directed to the minister the following question:
Could the minister tell me which government services will be housed in that building?
The building in question is the one which was to be erected at Chicoutimi.
The minister answered:

The post office, the customs office, the unemployment insurance commission office and, I am told, other government services.
I suppose that the idea is to centralize, in this new building, the different federal offices that now exist at Chicoutimi.
He would know now which departments might use this building.
On October 27, 1953, the present minister wrote me the following:
Dear Mr. Gagnon:
In reply to your letter of the 15th instant concerning the proposed public building at Chicoutimi, I must inform you that we do not expect to be able to call for tenders with regard to that building before the spring of 1954.
Please believe me, dear Mr. Gagnon.

Robert H. Winters.

An item of $250,000 was approved

The situation there, Mr. Chairman, as I recall it, is that although there was that amount in the estimates last year we found this year when compiling the estimates that we were not ready to go ahead with the building. The.'

plans had not been prepared. At the same time the postmaster indicated to me that he would like to study the whole matter of postal services in the area, and until such time as that is done we shall not be able to proceed with the building.
On May 14, 1954, I made the following remarks to the hon. Postmaster General:
Last year parliament approved a $250,000 appropriation for construction of a public building in Chicoutimi. A few days ago, when I asked the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) where this project stood and why there was no mention of that amount in this year's estimates, he answered that the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) had told him that he would like to make a survey of postal services in that district and that his department was not in a position to proceed with this building before this survey was ended.
I would therefore like the Postmaster General to tell me what point has been reached in this survey and whether he will soon make a report to his colleague, the Minister of Public Works.
The minister knows full well that for the past twenty years and more the people of Chicoutimi, through civil authorities and chambers of commerce, have been requesting the erection of a suitable building. Present accommodation is inadequate, considering the growing needs of those people. A few years ago some land was acquired for that purpose. I know that the minister is well acquainted with Chicoutimi and that he also has some good friends there. I would therefore like him to tell me, when he speaks of his department, what his plans are with regard to Chicoutimi.
Here is part of the answer given by the Postmaster General as reported at page 4763 of Hansard:
As far as the Chicoutimi project is concerned, I do not remember whether the plan called for a building to accommodate various federal departments or whether it was only to be a postal station. I know that we had to revise this project and hold back for further study. X will look further into the matter and will be glad to give more detailed information to the hon. member.
I must add that the project has not been abandoned but that it is simply under further consideration.

I hereby acknowledge receipt of your letter of September 21 regarding the construction of a public building in Chicoutimi.
Since returning from my trip I have had the opportunity of discussing this matter with the Postmaster General and other departments concerned. X can tell you that I have asked the building construction branch of my department to undertake the preparation of plans for this building.
Yours very truly,
Robert H. Winters.

The situation will not be lost sight of with regard to the difficulties mentioned. However it will be impossible to proceed with the immediate construction of a building in Chicoutimi, appro-

priations for this purpose not having been included in our departmental estimates for the coming fiscal year.

Robert H. Winters.
I made it a point, Mr. Chairman, to read part of the correspondence exchanged between the Minister of Public Works, the Postmaster General and the Chicoutimi chamber of commerce, as well as certain appeals I made in the house, in order to show all the delay in this matter and the excuses put forth for not remedying this situation, which has become unbearable.
I wish to assure the Minister of Public Works that should he be kind enough to pay us a visit at Chicoutimi, he would be received as a friend and I am convinced that having seen for himself the acute situation with which we are faced, he would immediately grant us this public building for which the land was purchased some years ago.
Here is what the Progres du Saguenay, a daily newspaper published in our district, had to say on December 22, 1954, about the postal service in the city of Chicoutimi:
We would like to see the embarrassment of the Postmaster General if, during a stay in Chicoutimi, he had to send his Christmas parcels through the local post office. He would very likely do the utmost without delay to correct an unbearable situation. A visit to the post office, facing the cathedral, during the rush period, would show the congestion there is in that building. The number of wickets being insufficient, people have to queue up and must wait as long as half an hour to unload their parcels which become exceedingly heavy. We are not criticizing the service given by the postal employees: they are doing the best they can under the circumstances and the postmaster has enough employees to provide the best service he can in the existing building but the people cannot tolerate indefinitely such a situation.
The building of a new post office at Chicoutimi has definitely been agreed upon, but the necessary appropriations have not yet been voted. Let us hope that they will be at the next session.
One can readily understand, Mr. Chairman, why the people of Chicoutimi are so much in favour of decentralization of powers and provincial autonomy.
They know how difficult it is to get anything but statutory grants from the federal government.
We can count on our fingers the favours bestowed upon us by Ottawa since confederation, while the favours granted us by the government of our own province, especially in the past 10 years, have changed the appearance of our cities and even of our smallest villages. Our district is among those that pay the most taxes to Ottawa but, on

the other hand, it is perhaps the one which receives the least in return.
We should be treated, not with more generosity because there is no such thing in Ottawa, but with more justice.
The taxpayers of Chicoutimi deserve more sympathetic attention from the government and I think the time has come to recognize it. Besides, I am satisfied that the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works are well disposed towards us and that they will at last grant our requests.

Mr. Chairman, in common with other members I regret the Postmaster General has not yet been able to return to his duties. I do hope however that he will have a speedy recovery and will soon be back with us.
I have a matter that I wish to bring up. I have taken it up with the department on other occasions. I am prompted to do it again because I have received a petition, and when I have finished with it I am going to send it over to the Acting Postmaster General. It has to do with my request some time ago for an airmail service to Norway House. I do not need to go into it. In the wintertime they get mail from Winnipeg, via Wabowden, and into Norway House. In the summertime they have to use the Keenora, which visits there once a week. This petition asks the department to do something about getting first class mail into Norway House more often than just once a week.
During the freeze-up and the break-up when the bombardier and the boat cannot operate, there are times when they get no mail service. I know that the weather is to blame for that.
That happens in my riding.

Yes, you and I should get together on this thing.
The plane that carries the mail during that period is quite a large one. It has been suggested by some people, who should know, that a lighter plane could land there with first class mail. They had the unfortunate experience this year of being without mail for some 5 weeks. The minister was surprised at that, but it was true.
I am not going to elaborate on it. There are 70 signatures on the petition. I know many of these people personally. They are reliable and good Canadians. They are worthy of the minister's consideration in an effort to get first class mail in there by air. If the
Supply-Post Office
Acting Postmaster General and his parliamentary assistant lived in Norway House they would have to prepare their mail on Monday night to get it away on Tuesday morning. That permits the mail to get into Winnipeg on Saturday afternoon. Because the mail arrives on Saturday afternoon you cannot possibly get a reply until the following week when the boat returns.
Let me give an example of how it works. A letter posted in Norway House on Monday, May 23, leaves that place on the 24th or the 25th, depending on the weather conditions. It reaches Winnipeg on Saturday afternoon, May 28. The offices or the wholesale houses receive it on May 30. At that time the mail bags for Norway House are already on the way to the station or to Selkirk. Therefore, that mail does not leave Winnipeg until the following week, and an answer will have to wait until Monday, June 6. It will reach Norway House on June 8 or June 9.
Some people seem to think that Norway House is away back from civilization, but let me draw the committee's attention to this. There are about 1,800 people in and around that district. The population is composed of Indians, half-breeds and white people. There is a large up-to-date settlement; there is a large new hospital there, an Indian agency, a detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, 2 boarding schools, missions representing the different churches, and also different day schools and a few stores. Surely, a community of this size is entitled to better mail service than they are getting at the present time.
If you look at a map of my constituency you will see that not very far from Norway House is Cross Lake, God's Lake and Oxford House. These places get an airmail service. There is also Island Lake, which receives an airmail service twice a week. I am advancing these arguments in an effort to get the department to give this matter further consideration. I appeal to the Acting Postmaster General and the parliamentary assistant, and ask them to look this over to see if it is not possible to give Norway House an airmail service for first class mail in the near future.

Order. May I take a moment of the time of the committee to express my views on this particular subject? It seems to me that under the estimates of the Post Office Department, or of any other service department, the inadequacy, or the non-existence, of certain facilities must surely be a subject which is within the ambit of the resolution that we are discussing. I can understand that if the Department of Public Works had undertaken the construction of a building for the Post Office Department and some member wished to criticize the manner in which that construction was being carried on, or the speed, it would come under the estimates of the Department of Public Works. But if the hon. member is, as I think he is, dealing with non-existent facilities which he is asking the Post Office Department to bring in, then I find it impossible to rule that he would be out of order; because, if the building is not under construction, then it seems to me it surely is not within the ambit of the Department of Public Works. I hardly see how one can discuss under the Department of Public Works the construction of post offices which the Department of Public Works has not been instructed to construct. Therefore, while I can see that it is very desirable that all members should hold their criticisms and their

requests down to those things which the Postmaster General can bring into effect, I cannot rule that the discussion of the need for improving or enlarging the post office facilities is out of order in a discussion of the estimates of the Post Office Department. I cannot rule a discussion of the need for improved or enlarged post office facilities to be out of order during a discussion of estimates of the Post Office Department, but I think perhaps one would be justified in saying that members would at least be indicating their co-operation if the need for the same building was not discussed under more than one department.

abide by your ruling and I am also not going to tramp on the toes of the minister.
