The space in which they have to work is deplorable. As I say, I have brought photographs to show the conditions.
I thought we were getting somewhere when I saw an item in the estimates. I am wondering now whether the officials of the Post Office Department changed their minds and decided that this post office was not needed. I will have to ask the Minister of Public Works what he did with that $25,000. During the last election they even had blueprints of the post office and, believe me, that did not help me any. This year there is no money being voted for a post office. I hope the Acting Postmaster General will look into this matter and recommend that Selkirk be given a new post office. The present building could be used to advantage for the R.C.M.P. and the Indian affairs branch. It would be good business to do that and to give Selkirk a new post office.

Mr. Chairman, I imagine that there is no one who rises to speak on the post office estimates but thinks of the employees working for that department, the service which they are rendering and the efforts which they are putting into their jobs. That is particularly so because the Post Office Department, next to the Department of National Defence, is

the largest employer of labour in the government. I think we have a particular respect for these employees of the post office when we realize some of the difficulties under which they labour and remember that the top man of their department has not been present in the house for some time. I am sure we all regret the unfortunate illness of the Postmaster General, for whom we have great respect. When you think about it for a few minutes you will perhaps wonder what would happen if the present status of the Postmaster General and the Acting Postmaster General were reversed. It is just possible that in that case both the Post Office Department and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration might be better off.
There was one thing in the remarks of the parliamentary assistant to the Postmaster General that surprised me quite a little, because to me it flies practically in the face of something we were told last year at the time the proposed and now effective increase in postal rates was being discussed. At that time the Postmaster General, as reported on page 1102 of Hansard of January 14, 1954, was referring to certain cost increases which he foresaw for his department, and he went on to say:
These three items alone amount to $13,500,000. Expected net revenues from the increase in postage rates will be approximately $14 million, leaving only $500,000 to take care of possible normal increases in the price of basic materials and services which are essential for the operation of the postal service.
At that time the Postmaster General was crying poverty before the house. He said he simply had to have this increase in postal rates because if it did not come along his department was going to operate under a tremendous deficit. He was calculating that the increase in the postal rates would be just sufficient to permit him to end up on a break-even basis. If you read through the discussion of those several days you come away with the impression that even with the increase the post office was going to have a pretty tough time making ends meet.
The estimates originally tabled show a surplus for the present year of something over $6 million while the statement made earlier this afternoon indicates a surplus of approximately $5 million. Of course it is all hedged about with verbiage about public buildings, franking and various other things. When the Postmaster General was crying his tale of woe before the house last year there was no mention of those particular items. It is only now when the Post Office Department finds that it is wrong in its estimate that they come before us and
Supply-Post Office
attempt to explain away their faulty figuring. They surround the estimate with this other material which apparently has been thought up on the spur of the moment as an excuse.
In some respects I think we can feel very glad that there is this surplus, provided it is the result of more efficient operation in the post office. In that case it is a welcome situation which is far different from most other departments of government.
I would rather hope that with this surplus it might be possible for the government to examine again the question of their postal rates to see whether some reduction in some rates would not be possible.
We have had continuing promises for many years that as soon as the government found itself in a position to reduce taxation it would do so. They gave us a small example of that this year. If they were really and genuinely speaking their minds on this subject, let them give us another example. Let them take this $5 million surplus in the operations of the Post Office Department and follow through with a reduction in postal rates.
Having said that, I go on to make one or two comments on the post office and some of its operation. First I should like to deal with a situation which I think is particularly iniquitous because it is a direct reversal of what we in this party would like to think is the right way for a government to operate, that is to treat all people alike. We like to think that that is the principle upon which a government should operate. We like to think particularly that the government should treat all its employees alike.
If a man holds a job in one centre he should receive the same treatment and prerogatives as he would receive if he held the same job in another centre. We see no particular reason why there should be one set of rules and one set of standards for a man who happens to live and work for the government in Montreal and another set for a man holding the same position in Toronto. Yet I defy the gentlemen who sit over there on the opposite side of the chamber presenting these estimates to the committee to stand up and say that in the post office they have not the situation in which certain men who occupy exactly similar positions within the post office structure are being given varying treatment according to the locality in which they work.
To bolster this statement I am going to have to set it out in detail. I set it out for the benefit of the committee. Over a period of a couple of months I have tried to discuss it with the officials of the post office. I did

Supply-Post Office
not want to bring it before the House of Commons because it has always been my experience that once a minister takes a position in the house, no matter how stupid it is, he will never retreat from that position. However, sometimes you can get even a stupid minister-and they exist, Mr. Chairman-to see reason if you discuss the thing with him outside the house where his mistakes do not have to be brought. before the people of Canada as a whole. That was my hope in this instance; but as far as I can see, I have not made much progress.
The situation is this. With the advent of the five-day week in the post office and with the department's desire to continue six-day-a-week mail delivery, it became necessary to employ certain other people who would, on a rotating basis, fill in on route after route as the regular men went off for their sixth day holiday. In order to get those men the department went to its present employees and offered them the opportunity for these particular positions. In order to make the position attractive, they gave them a title which, if my memory serves me rightly, was that of supervisory letter carrier. In connection with this matter it is important to remember that although a different title is - attached to this job, the function is, without any change whatever, similar to that of the normal mail carrier, save that in the one case the mail carrier remains on the same route and in the other-supervisory letter carrier is the name of the function-he will rotate from one route to another.
Through certain circumstances which I will not go into here most of these supervisory letter carrier positions appeared to be more attractive to the newcomers to the department. By accepting that position, the newcomer to the department could get a sudden increase in salary. It brought him no higher than the men who had been in the department for a number of years but it brought him up to their level. That perhaps was the principal interest of the newcomer in applying for these positions. The result was that after a period of time the department found, first, that most of these supervisory letter carrier positions, for which applications had been made, were being applied for by newcomers to the department. Second, they found that they were not getting sufficient applications to fill all their positions. Thus, they decided to do something which I think was quite unfair.
In this connection I turn now to a series of three announcements or bulletins from the post office which dealt with these positions of supervisory letter carriers. The first one went out on February 19, 1954, and it said

in effect-the government never speaks quite in this way-"We need supervisory letter carriers; here are the details of the position. The men who fill that position will have no preference in relationship to choosing their vacations over the rest of the letter carrier staff".
A week later, on February 26, the government completely reversed its position, this time issuing a bulletin saying that those who apply for the position of supervisory letter carrier and are accepted will have a preference over the remainder of the letter carrier staff in respect of their vacations.
As I have already indicated, the majority of these supervisory letter carriers were comparative newcomers to the service, and the effect of this second bulletin was to give them preference in choosing their vacation period over many men who had been in the service for 10 years, 15 years or 20 years as letter carriers, who had families, who had vacation plans and who had every reason-[DOT] both because of length of service and because of personal position-to have prior consideration in respect of choice of their vacations. This was so obvious to the entire postal service across Canada and its officials that the holler which went up was simply tremendous.
Finally the department came out with one of the most amazing bulletins-for anybody who believes in decent treatment of employees-that I can imagine. It is dated March 16. It deals with this same subject and in effect it says this. I have a French version here and that is why I say "in effect", since I am not quoting directly from the English. In effect it says: If it is possible to get enough good letter carrier supervisors without giving them any preference with regard to vacations, you do not need to give them any preference with regard to vacation. But in the localities where it is impossible to recruit the necessary number of good letter carrier supervisors without giving them a preference in vacation time, we will give them this preference with regard to vacation.
What has happened since then, Mr. Chairman? In Toronto letter carrier supervisors and mail men-the ordinary letter carriers -select together from the same list in order of seniority. If a man is a letter carrier supervisor but has only five years of service he will not get a choice of vacation dates until an ordinary letter carrier with six years or ten years of service has had his choice of vacation. That situation applies in the great majority of locations across Canada. But in a minor number of cases, including Montreal, in order to bludgeon and

to force the letter carriers into accepting these positions, the Post Office Department has chosen to give this preference in choice of vacation time-this preference which exists nowhere else except in these few localities across Canada-in respect of the letter carrier supervisor position, a job which is exactly the same as that of the letter carrier himself.
There are letter carriers by the hundreds- and I use that word advisedly-in the city of Montreal who have been in the service of the department for many years, who are being discriminated against. Because they are older men they have children who are going to school. They have perhaps got enough money together to be able to have a country home to which they like to go. These men are being deprived of their opportunity to take their vacations at a time when they can go with their families to their country homes in order that some newcomer to the department who has taken advantage of this particular situation to get a fast salary increase-and I have no objection to that whatsoever-may take his vacation in the months of July or August. It is .completely unfair and iniquitous. To cite two cities, a completely different set of standards applies to letter carriers in Toronto and letter carriers in Montreal.
In the course of my discussions on this matter I never saw, in my estimation, more uncomfortable people than the departmental officials with whom I discussed it. We had interesting discussions that were very helpful. I am grateful to them for their help, but right across the board, starting with the heads of the department who sit in the house, it seems that I have never been able to get any sort of satisfactory answer outside of the completely ruthless one that they have got to do this in order to force these men into these positions. That was the interpretation I placed on the information I got from them, and I have never been able to get any other answer.
Having dealt with that subject and placed it on the record, may I express the hope at this point that this inconsiderate, ruthless and inequitable attitude of the department will be changed and changed very quickly.
I should now like to say a few words about the post office savings bank which was dealt with at some length in the Woods and Gordon report of some note last year. I think hon. members will recall the recommendation in the Woods and Gordon report that the post office savings bank be discontinued. I should 50433-262
Supply-Post Office
like to quote one or two sentences from the report. It has this to say:
. . . other banking facilities are available in the communities of 18,670 of the 22,699 active depositors.
In other words, at that point they were making the argument that in most places across Canada facilities parallel to the post office savings bank are available. The report says further:
It is apparent therefore that the need for the facilities of the post office savings bank is not nearly as great as it used to be and we suggest that .the time may have come when it could be wound up without hardship to any large number of depositors.
Finally:
The annual cost ... of the post office savings bank is estimated to be $377,000.
Despite this report, the department subsequently decided to continue the operation of this largely unnecessary and certainly money losing function. In thinking about the matter the thought came to me first that if .we could suggest an alternative means by which facilities similar to the post office savings bank could be made available to the Canadian people generally at a figure substantially less than the current cost of the post office savings bank, we might be able to persuade the government to get out of this small banking business. I want to make it quite plain at this juncture that, while I think the government has some responsibility to lead in the provision of certain services, I feel equally strongly that when private enterprise is in a position to provide those services adequately it is time for the government to get out of the service. They certainly should not continue to operate them at a loss involving such an expense to the taxpayers as in this case.
Therefore I put forward this thought for the possible consideration of the Postmaster General, the Acting Postmaster General and the parliamentary assistant to the Postmaster General. In 1952 there were only 167,000 deposits made in the post office savings bank. That is the last figure I have. All the department needs to do is to agree to carry these deposits, properly insured and properly registered, from the post offices to any chartered bank branch in Canada without cost. They can then get out of the banking business in this field tomorrow and leave post office savings bank depositors in exactly the same position as they are now.
In other words, what I am suggesting is that the post office savings bank would drop out of the operation. Its accounts and operations would be placed with the chartered banking system of Canada. People who now bank with the post office savings bank would

Supply-Post Office
bank with a chartered bank. In cases where people cannot go directly to the bank they now have the privilege of sending their money through the mails, as we all know, but if we want them to be on a basis comparable to the present post office savings bank it may be necessary for the post office to carry these funds to a bank without charge. The interesting thing is that if the Post Office Department did that the charge incurred by the department for the cost of the postage and registration would be about $25,000 for the whole operation against the $377,000 that they are now paying.
An alternative suggestion, which I just mention, is that a person might be allowed to deposit his money with the post office, obtain a receipt and send the receipt to the bank which would in turn, on depositing the receipt with the post office, be reimbursed for the amount. The point I am trying to make in putting forward these two ideas is that the department should take another look at the post office savings bank with the thought in mind of seeing that the depositors will still get the services they are now getting but will get them through some established banking operation so that the government can get out of the business.
I should like to say a few words about twice-a-day mail deliveries. I do not agree with the attitude of the Postmaster General and the department that once a day mail delivery is genuinely satisfactory or acceptable to the people of Canada. In the statement made this afternoon it was said that the number of complaints with respect to this matter has been reduced. Of course they have been reduced. After people have complained and complained and complained for four or five years they finally throw up their hands in disgust and say: There is no use any more; we will stop complaining.
I can remember that when the income tax was first raised substantially not too many years ago there was a great deal of discussion and tremendous antipathy towards the move. We have reached the point now where we all realize, I think, that the incidence of taxation is terribly heavy, but you might say that we have learned to live with it a little bit. We do not like it but we know there is no use complaining because it is going to be crammed down our throats anyway. I think that has been the attitude of the people of Canada towards this one-a-day mail delivery. I suggest this thought in that connection to the Postmaster General. Why do we not have two-a-day mail deliveries five days a week? At the present time we give a mail delivery in most residential areas once a day, and that is six deliveries a week. If
[Mr. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace) .1
you gave two deliveries a day for five days, that would be 10 deliveries a week, which is an extra service.
The interesting thing about it is that if you examine it carefully you will find your costs for the two deliveries a day five days a week would be very little more if any more than the cost of the type of service that is now given. The operation of the department on Saturday would be reduced to a minimum. Sortage charges, overtime pay for clerks and many other things connected with Saturday operation would be substantially reduced. My information and my analysis lead me to the conclusion we could have two-a-day mail delivery five days a week on a very sound basis. I believe the people of Canada would be more satisfied with that. I feel they would far rather have 10 deliveries a week than six deliveries a week. I believe that in an era when we have come almost universally to recognize that the five-day week is in existence, the Post Office Department would receive general public approval if they realized that as well.
I regret, Mr. Chairman, that a question of mine of May 11 has not been answered. I am rather interested in it. In the last six months or so the Post Office Department seems to have been subjected to a rash of thefts and robberies. My question of May 11 asked for certain information concerning thefts and robberies over the past year or so. I am amazed, first, that it was found necessary to make it an order for return. I am very surprised that the post office was not in a position, on as important a matter as money being stolen from office after office across Canada, to give an immediate answer to that question. But no, they bury it by means of making it an order for return. The question affects only one department, so there could be no reason for letting it stand for more than two weeks without an answer. The only inference I can draw, Mr. Chairman, is that the Post Office Department does not know how much money has been stolen from it, where it has been stolen, who is being charged with those thefts or what sort of success is being achieved in curbing the thefts.
I think that is a particularly poor situation for a department which has had something of the order of a quarter of a million dollars stolen from it in the last six months. Among other things, this department found it necessary to engage a man who finally turned out, only a couple of months afterwards, to be one of Canada's 10 most wanted criminals.

Here is a release from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police dated January 27, 1955, which says:
John Keith MacDonald, 46, an ex-insurance agent, has been added to Canada's most wanted criminals list. John Keith MacDonald has been identified as John Clealand Wallace Black who is wanted in connection with the $44,500 missing from the post office at Britannia Beach, B.C., on December 17, 1954.
MacDonald, under the name of Black, was employed in the post office as a clerk.
In other words, we have now reached the point where the Post Office Department, handling tremendous sums of money like this, is apparently letting creep into its staff- who are ' almost all among the finest people in Canada-criminals who are prepared to steal money from the department. Do you not think that indicates poor supervision somewhere along the line, poor care in the selection of certain employees or a loose examination of the records of the people who are allowed to handle post office funds?
Perhaps it is the result of patronage.

My
hon. friend points out that perhaps this man came in under patronage. There are lots of such people in the post office who certainly did not go through the normal civil service channels. I hope, though, that even the Liberal party is not accustomed to patronizing some of Canada's most wanted criminals. I have a lot against these men on the treasury benches, but I do not think they would go that far-at least, not in between elections.
There is one point I should like to bring before the house. On March 25, I asked another question concerning the machinations of the post offices in Montreal and Toronto in connection with the T-4 returns. I am not going to go into details on that because I am coming towards the end of my time. I do want to express my regret that the question has not been answered up until now. I should like the Acting Postmaster General to lay before the house the information which I know he now has in that connection, and explain to us why it is that the government must break its own rules. In other words, the Department of National Revenue prescribed that certain returns must be in by a certain time, and a penalty was attached to failure to observe this provision. Then the post office, daddling along again probably without proper supervision or control, breaks the rules of another government department, delays these returns and generally causes considerable inconvenience to the employees in a number of Canadian cities.
It was interesting, Mr. Chairman, when they did make the return in the province 50433-262i
Supply-Post Office
of Quebec, to find that they got around to filing the federal government return first and then the provincial return. I do not know whether or not that is any indication of this government's attitude towards these two income tax systems. I mention that as well, and I think we might have an explanation of it.
In the course of this talk, Mr. Chairman, I have pointed out first the woolly-headedness of the Post Office Department in coming before this house last year and asking for an increase in postal rates, at which time they cried poor mouth and indicated they would have no surplus. Then later they come along and inform us that they have made over $5 million. I have pointed out the unfairness of their labour policy in respect to vacations for letter carriers in certain parts of this country. I have pointed out ways in which they might quite legitimately and quite properly give the same service to the people of Canada in respect of the post office savings bank and save themselves $325,000. I have pointed out the way in which they could restore the two-a-day mail delivery over a period of five days a week to the centres which are now deprived of it with very little, if any, increase in the cost of providing the service. I have pointed out a situation that is rotten in respect of thefts from the department and the way in which they are allowing the occasional person of doubtful record to creep into their ranks and sully the reputation of 50,000 of Canada's most devoted civil servants. Then, I have pointed out the' regrettable situation in connection with the filing of their own T-4 returns.
I think what I have said will suffice for this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to discuss more than one matter under this vote. I am not going to ask the Acting Postmaster General for a new post office at Vancouver. It is now being built, and we appreciate it very much.
However, there is one matter I most certainly wish to discuss this afternoon, a matter which I consider of the utmost importance -of such importance that I am going to be most careful and deliberate in anything I shall say about it. Sir, the use of the mails is very important; it is a great trust. I am hoping that after I have finished, the Acting Postmaster General or the parliamentary assistant will be able to give us some information.
In order to introduce the subject I have in mind perhaps I should give some background material. There has developed in Canada

The Royal Assent
and in the United States a practice of sending goods or magazines to citizens, even though such goods or magazines have not been ordered.
I have known this for some considerable time. My understanding of the law is that if one has not ordered goods or has not subscribed to a magazine, he does not have to pay. However, I am afraid there are many people in this country-I would say even a majority of people-who do not know that they are protected by the law which says that if they have not ordered goods or subscribed to a magazine they do not have to pay.
However, there has been an unfortunate development in Canada in that some companies are sending out goods and magazines without orders or subscriptions, and then forwarding letters through the mail demanding payment. I have heard about this often, but only recently did it come to my close attention. Someone may ask why I discuss this matter under the estimates of the Post Office Department. I do so because there is connected with it the use of the mails in Canada.
I have said I am going to be very careful and deliberate. I shall speak from my own knowledge-and not only that because I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has had a similar experience. I say, sir, that in my estimation Her Majesty's mails in Canada are being used for what I call indirect blackmail, and that as a result many citizens of Canada are being placed in an invidious position, not because of Her Majesty's postal service but because of the use being made of it.
I would ask the Acting Postmaster General and the parliamentary assistant whether the law in Canada, and the regulations under that law, are adequate to take care of what is now taking place in this country. If not, will the government bring in the required amendments to the act or the regulations?
Let me place on record my own experience, to show what is happening. About two years ago someone-I do not know who- sent to Life magazine an order for a 12-months subscription to be delivered to me. I do not know who did that. I received Life magazine for 12 months and at the end of that time received a letter from Life, 540 North Michigan avenue, Chicago, Illinois, telling me that my subscription had expired.
I wrote the magazine saying that I had not subscribed and did not wish to have the magazine sent to me. It continued to come. They wrote me again saying, "You have not renewed your subscription", ignoring completely the fact that I never had one. They told me that I owed them a certain amount

of money, and I replied "I have never subscribed to your magazine, nor have I renewed a subscription. I have told you once that I do not want to have the magazine sent to me." It continued to come, and I received another letter to which I replied as I had replied before. Those communications were from the United States.
But, Mr. Acting Postmaster General, last week I got something different. And what I received last week brings this matter within the purview of Her Majesty's mails in Canada. The letter I received last week was signed by a man named Charles A. Palmer, and the letterhead bore the name of Life magazine, of the United States. This letter from Charles A. Palmer, credit manager, enclosed a business reply envelope addressed to Life, Post Office Box 160, Toronto, Ontario, for the attention of Mr. Charles A. Palmer. So now it is strictly a Canadian matter, and a Canadian postal matter.
Sir, I want to read to you the letter I received, after having for months said I did not want the publication. I never sent for the publication; I have never taken any subscription to the publication. This is the letter I received through Her Majesty's mail:
I am very sorry that I have to write to you-

At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

At the time we adjourned this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, in order that the House of Commons could attend at the other place, I was drawing to the attention of the committee a factor which I thought was of importance, namely that of using Her Majesty's mails for a purpose which I said- and I will repeat it-I thought was indirect blackmail. I had outlined to the committee a procedure which was being followed by companies in sending not only goods but magazines to citizens of Canada, then sending them a bill-even although they have not ordered the goods or the magazines-and then demanding payment. This afternoon I pointed out that this is followed up, to my own knowledge, by three letters from the United States. At the time of adjournment I had pointed out that on the fourth occasion it is a letter strictly from and in Canada, thus bringing the matter within the complete jurisdiction of the postal services of Canada.
At the time of adjournment I was just starting to read a letter which I received only one week ago about a publication which I never ordered, and never subscribed to. I wrote three times to Life magazine in Chicago, Illinois, saying that I did not want it. Yet from Toronto last week, under the name of Charles A. Palmer, I received a letter. Not only did I receive a letter but I received an envelope saying that it should be sent to "Life, P.O. Box 160, Toronto, Ontario. Attention: Charles A. Palmer". If you desire me to do so, Mr. Chairman, I will file that envelope with you. I also received a bill. I have it right here and I will file it, Mr. Chairman, if you desire me to do so. This bill says "Amount due, $7.87" and "Due for copies mailed, $2.60". This, sir, is from Toronto. Here is the letter sent through Her Majesty's
Supply-Post Office
mail on something I never ordered, with a bill which I do not know anything about. Here is the letter:
I am very sorry I have to write you this letter. Up to now we thought you really wanted Life- and had just put off or forgotten to pay for your subscription.
Mr. Chairman, I never subscribed to that magazine in my life, but this is what I received:
But now that your account has remained unpaid so long that we have had to stop sending you Life- now that we are billing you only for copies already served . . .
Mr. Chairman, the letter talks about "copies already served". I have said I will file, if you require it, the bill sent me for $2.60 for copies mailed but also due, $7.87. I quote again:
For we are members of the Publishers National Credit Service; and, as members, we have assumed a very definite obligation to other publishers and to all other business houses that extend mail order credit.
Sir, I am asking you to note that term "mail order credit" because I am going to refer to it in a few moments. Again I quote:
And that obligation makes it impossible for us just to forget the small bill you have owed us over these last few months, for each account on our books is closely investigated by the credit auditors.
Somehow I can't help feeling that our not receiving your cheque or money order for so small a sum must have been a mistake. For it almost never happens that the kind of person who would be interested in Life consciously defaults his bill . . .
If your failure to send your payment was just an oversight, will you please let me have your cheque in the enclosed envelope, marked for my personal attention, by return mail?
And "by return mail" is underlined. The letter is signed by Charles A. Palmer of Toronto.
Mr. Chairman, 1 have had a remarkable experience since I adjourned the debate when the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod knocked on the door when I was speaking. Since then a number of members of parliament have come to me and said that they have had letters of a similar nature. I asked them, "What have you done with them?'" They were not all from the same company.. They all have told these people where they could go and, as I did, just how they could! get there. But, sir, we are members oft' parliament. Perhaps we know something about the law. But if letters of this kindt are being sent to members of parliament demanding payment and casting aspersions on our characters, I wonder how many thousands of people in Canada-who perhaps; do not know the law as we do and who. perhaps can be intimidated as we cannot be-

Supply-Post Office
-are getting letters of the same kind, demanding payment on something they have never ordered, and being sent through Her Majesty's mail.
