speechtext: Order. I have hesitated to interrupt the hon. member but I have been waiting with some interest to see how he would connect his remarks with the estimates of the Post Office Department. He has related at some length letters which he has received through the mails, but so far I do not see that he has shown in what way the Post Office Department would enter into this matter or how his remarks are related to the estimates of the department. I would ask the hon. member to relate his remarks to resolution No. 334, administration of the Post Office Department.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, I thought I had made that very clear when I began my remarks this afternoon. First of all I had to give the background of the picture and show what was happening. I pointed out that demands for payment, which I called and still call indirect blackmail, were being sent through Her Majesty's mails. The letter I have just read came through Her Majesty's mails. When I began my remarks this afternoon I asked if the Acting Postmaster General or the parliamentary assistant could inform the house whether it was permissible for Her Majesty's mails to be used along the lines I have been outlining. I have related the matter completely to the estimates now before us.
There is one other phase of the use of the mails for this purpose which can be very serious and detrimental to anybody who receives through the mails this kind of letter demanding payment and enclosing a bill for something never ordered or subscribed for. Information that payment is refused goes to a credit association, and there are such associations in every province of Canada. Such information about failure to make payment can hurt the credit of anyone in this dominion. Therefore I think this is an important matter. As I said only a few moments ago, I have discovered I am not the only one who has had this experience. A number of members have encountered the same thing. I have been told by three members of parliament that Time magazine is doing the same thing as Life magazine. Therefore I ask the question now, and I think it is important in the interests of the people of Canada, whether or not the postal law and regulations can prevent the Canadian mails being used for this kind of thing. If not, will the Acting Postmaster General take under advisement the amendment of the law or regulations to

stop this practice on the part largely of United States companies operating through agencies in Canada, and which is now prevalent in this country.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I was attending the external affairs committee and I am not aware of what course the debate has followed. However, I want to bring to the attention of the acting minister and his assistant a couple of matters I was asked to raise, and as usual I will be quite brief. Our letter carriers perform a very essential and necessary service and the amount of labour involved in it is not appreciated by many people. They walk miles every day going up and down steps from house to house. In my constituency their difficulties are rather above average. We have advantages and disadvantages on account of living in Kootenay West.
In the cities of Nelson and Trail the letter carriers have to climb hundreds of steps daily going from one street to another and therefore the performance of their duties is somewhat more arduous than is the general case throughout Canada. I know that their organization has made representations urging an increase in their rates of pay and improvement of their working conditions. I am simply going to ask that sympathetic consideration be given to these representations and that every consideration be taken of the burdensome nature of their employment compared with many other jobs in the civil service.
The other matter I want to raise has to do with what I think is a quite unnecessary burden placed upon the letter carriers by many companies. Letter carriers and postmasters tell me there is an increasing number of heavy catalogues, booklets of various kinds and other reading material going through the mails. Quite recently it was brought to my attention that Reader's Digest produced a special booklet and sent thousands of copies into my constituency. Each booklet weighed one pound, eight ounces, and the local letter carriers had to lug them around and make trip after trip to dispose of them. The whole staff was completely exhausted when that day's work was completed.
I suggest the Post Office Department should make some better arrangements and find some way of having this heavier material delivered without causing this completely unnecessary burden on letter carriers. I understand that formerly this only occurred at infrequent intervals, but now the carriers are repeatedly being burdened with heavy catalogues, booklets and things of that sort. I do not know what to suggest. Possibly

a card could be mailed from the post office to the person who is to receive the publication or some arrangement could be made for their distribution by freight or express. I was asked to bring these two matters to the attention of the acting minister, and I trust he will give them his usual serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Kootenay West, I was also busy this afternoon with committee work. I too do not know just what trend the discussion has taken. I want to say at the outset I have had the very finest co-operation from the officials of the department in all matters I have brought to their attention. But there is one matter I believe must go to the ministerial level for attention, the question of the differential in rates of pay between various classes of post offices. There are perhaps four post offices in Kootenay East that are grade 9 offices. The rates of pay for clerks in those offices begin at $2,010 a year and reach a maximum of $2,760 while postal clerks in the larger offices begin at $2,400 and reach a maximum of $3,360. I believe that the clerks in the smaller offices take the same civil service examination and are required to know as much about post office business and the distribution of mail to various countries as clerks in the larger offices. In the cities where the larger offices are, the cost of living is much lower in most cases. In East Kootenay, for instance, the men on prevailing rates are paid on the basis of rates in the mining and lumbering industry. Local conditions require a higher rate of pay for the employees to maintain equality with the local residents. Of course, the cost of groceries is very much higher than in the larger centres. It is for that reason I feel the clerks in the smaller grade 9 post offices should at least receive a rate comparable to that received by the clerks in the larger centres. I hope the minister will take that into consideration.

There are one or two observations I should like to make on this first item. Last year a great deal was said about the introduction of the 40-hour week and the government used that as one of the reasons for introducing an increase in postal rates. This year the parliamentary assistant referred to the 40-hour week and gave us some figures of the additional cost to the post office as well as the number of new employees resulting from the introduction of the 40-hour week. Last year there was some doubt in the minds of many of us as to just what the 40-hour week was going to be, particularly in view of the fact the Postmaster General seemed to feel that it meant
Supply-Post Office
a normal working period of 40 hours, followed by an overtime period paid for at regular rates of pay.
This matter was brought up last year, but we did not get any clear-cut satisfactory answers. I am not satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that there has been any improvement in this regard during the past year. I am sure hon. members received a letter dated February 9 from the federated association of letter carriers, branch No. 3, Hamilton, Ontario, dealing with the situation in one of our large postal areas in Canada. From the information contained in this letter over the signature of Fred Bimson, secretary treasurer, the postal officials asked the employees of the Montreal post office to vote on a plebiscite to determine whether or not they were in favour of working a six-day week, and for the hours worked in excess of the five-day week they were to be paid at an hourly rate equal to their salaries.
Now, when that plebiscite was held the letter carriers revealed quite clearly by their vote that they did not favour the proposed changes in their working conditions. However, in spite of the fact the letter carriers voted down the proposition put forward by the postal officials the department nevertheless went ahead with their plans. They ignored entirely the wishes of the employees in this regard. According to the information that we received in February last, the secretary of the federated association of letter carriers protested to departmental officials. He was informed-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
May
I say that the particular plebiscite to which the hon. member was referring was purely a local plebiscite. It was held in Montreal at the request of the employees and had no particular official sanction and no action was taken. We carried on as we had in the past.

I want to thank the parliamentary assistant for that bit of information. I had no way of knowing whether the plebiscite had been taken at the instigation of the Post Office Department or the employees. Nevertheless, the fact of the matter is a plebiscite was held, irrespective of the fact the initiative was taken by the employees, and apparently departmental officials were prepared to sound out the employees in that postal area. Those employees made it quite clear that they were not in favour of departing from the five-day 40-hour week. Notwithstanding the evident desire of the employees, the Post Office Department went ahead with the proposal. I am not suggesting it was made

Supply-Post Office
mandatory or compulsory, but the employees would be asked to work a sixth day and if they agreed to work a sixth day they would be paid only regular rates of pay.

May
I make this clear? The employees requested that this plebiscite be taken, and it was taken. In some areas a majority wanted the change and in other areas a majority did not want the change. The five-day 40-hour week was in effect before the plebiscite was taken and it was in effect afterwards. The vast majority of the employees throughout the city did not want any change. They wanted the five-day 40-hour week, and they still have it.

The thing I am concerned about is this. If it is the policy of the department to institute a 40-hour week in certain localities in Canada, then that is departmental policy. I gathered from the remarks made by the Postmaster General at the last session that he did not see anything wrong in the idea of asking postal employees to work extra hours at regular rates of pay. I recall asking the Postmaster General at that time whether he was not aware of the fact that under normal practice when an employee works in excess of the 40 hours then that employee should receive overtime pay at overtime rates of pay. The ordinary practice is to pay time and a half for overtime. That is the thing about which I am concerned. I am glad the parliamentary assistant has given more information about this matter.
I am still concerned about the status of the 40-hour week in the post office in those areas in Canada where the department has presumably adopted the 40-hour week. I feel that if the 40-hour week means anything, it means that the normal work week is 40 hours. Every employee who is required to work a single hour in excess of 40 hours is working overtime and should be paid for that at overtime rates of pay. If you do not pay time and a half for overtime, then it is not a proper 40-hour week. That is the thing about which I am concerned. I believe that when the Post Office Department or any other department of government institutes a 40-hour week, they ought to be prepared to pay employees who are asked to work overtime at overtime rates of pay. I hope when the parliamentary assistant speaks later he will deal with this point and inform the members of the committee whether or not the practice is to pay overtime rates of pay. Otherwise this boast of the 40-hour week is not entirely accurate.

Perhaps I may be permitted to interrupt the hon. member. I am

informed that the regulations with respect to the 40-hour week in the post office are precisely the same as they are in all other branches of the civil service where the 40-hour week is in force. Any change that might be made would apply to the civil service generally and would be made by the civil service commission. It would not be within the power of the Post Office Department to make any change, and therefore it would hardly seem to be an appropriate subject to deal with on these estimates and should be dealt with on the estimates of the civil service commission.
It seems to me that this afternoon the Acting Postmaster General has been on his feet three or four times stating points of order in which he has sought to circumscribe debate-
To the Post Office Department.

-by suggesting that we should bring this matter up or bring that matter up under the estimates of some other department. I suggest I would be out of order if I began to discuss the civil service as a whole. I am now dealing with post office employees because the estimates of the Post Office Department are now before the committee. What I am saying about postal employees certainly has an application in a wider field. But in an effort to be strictly in order I am confining my remarks to employees of the Post Office Department.

If I might interject once more, I would say that I have not the slightest desire to circumscribe the hon. member or any other hon. member. But there is a rule which says that the minister who is responsible for and can do something about a certain thing is the minister who ought to answer in that particular field.
I understand these regulations with respect to hours of work apply uniformly to all branches of the civil service. They could not be changed by the Postmaster General, nor could they be changed for the Post Office Department as a separate entity. Unless there were a general change of policy, whatever can be done would have to be done at the instigation of the responsible minister. I do not wish to circumscribe the hon. member, or anybody else, but it is certain that there is a large area over which the Postmaster General has responsibility, and that is the responsibility for which he is expected to answer in committee-and not with respect to things not within his jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the Acting Postmaster General must certainly be concerned about the esprit de

corps among post office employees. I am certain he is concerned about working conditions because, after all, the efficiency of his department depends upon good relationship between employers on the one hand and employees on the other. I suggest that if the Acting Postmaster General or the parliamentary assistant is anxious to bring about better conditions within the Post Office Department he might use his influence with the appropriate minister to bring about changes, not only in the Post Office Department, but in other departments of government as well.
There is one other aspect of working conditions among post office employees I wish to mention. I am referring to the matter of holidays. It will be recalled that at the last session holidays were used as an instrument of policy on the part of the post office to bring about certain desired effects so far as staff was concerned. It will be recalled that as a result of a change in policy at that time, which I understand has been modified since, certain employees who took certain jobs were given priority in the matter of holidays. As I say, it is my understanding that this policy has been modified to meet the wishes of the employees.
However, I think it is indicative of the type of thing we must always watch for in this department, when we find that this year the Post Office Department-and once again I am speaking of that department, but it has its broader application-is determined to use the annual holidays as a weapon to achieve certain results in the administration of the department.
Mention was made this afternoon of the rather humiliating proposal that civil servants who are late a certain number of hours shall have their holidays docked. I suggest to the acting minister that that is not the way to deal with the question of habitual lateness. If it is found that there are employees who are causing trouble and who, without reasonable excuse, are late habitually, then I think the proper method is to deal with each individual employee. But to pass a blanket regulation to cover all civil servants is an insult to them and a humiliation of the worst kind. The government is treating civil servants as parents might treat children. The threat is made that if employees are late so many times then, as a matter of policy, so much of their holiday time will be taken away. To my way of thinking that is a very shortsighted and foolish policy indeed.
As a matter of fact one civil servant who spoke to me about the matter said that he had not been late for work in the last seven years, but that he was greatly upset about
Supply-Post Office
this ruling. He was not concerned about himself, but rather with the principle involved. It is such a childish procedure for the government to say to civil servants en masse, "If you are late a certain number of hours you will lose that time from your holidays". I suggest that holidays are the right of employees, irrespective of the jobs they are doing; and that to use a man's or woman's holidays as a means of bringing about certain results in the day-to-day administration of the department is, to say the least, a mistake.
It seems to me there are a number of improvements that could be made in the Post Office Department, so far as working conditions are concerned. Hon. members may have noted the recommendations made by employees of this department a week or so ago, as publicized in the press. It would appear to me that those requests are quite reasonable and that the government should be giving favourable consideration to them. There are some matters I shall not deal with this evening, because I wish to be brief. There is, for example, the matter of longevity pay, as well as other proposals that are reasonable and which should commend themselves to the Acting Postmaster General. I hope those suggestions will be given consideration.
I wish to close on this note. Last year I suggested that we are always going to have little annoyances from time to time, so long as the government treats its employees in the present fashion. The answer of necessity must be that employees of the government, working through their organizations, must be free to bargain collectively with the government as the employer. I am certain all hon. members have come to accept the idea of collective bargaining, under which employees, through their organizations, meet with employers around the bargaining table and reach agreements mutually satisfactory. I think that is the only proper way to carry on negotiations and day-to-day discussions between employee and employer. I suggest the government ought to be giving serious consideration to keeping away from the idea that federal civil servants must simply beg for improvements in working conditions dealing with matters such as overtime, wage increases and the like. The only proper way is to say to the employees, "You have your organizations which are free to bargain on your behalf. We will meet around the table as equal partners, and we will arrive at a contract dealing with wages and with working conditions generally." I believe that is the only answer to improved relations between the government as an employer and its

Supply-Post Office
employees. It is something that we have to accept as normal and desirable in this country. Rather than always following the lead of other employers, the government should be setting the example. We have had arguments raised about the question of the 40-hour week in the post office. The 40-hour week should be made much wider in its scope; but the government takes the attitude, well, we are not going to institute the 40-hour week unless it is the normal practice in the area. In other words, the government as an employer is not going to set the example; it is going to adopt the 40-hour week in the areas where local conditions pretty much force it into that position.
I suggest that the government ought to be setting a high standard for other employers. One way in which they could do this is by revising their methods in dealing with employer-employee relationships. They should get the employees around the table and come to an agreement which would be applicable to both sides and mutually acceptable.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in connection with the matter which was brought up this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East. The hon. gentleman discussed a matter this afternoon and tonight which is giving some concern to many people. We are well aware in this country that some United States publishers are trying very hard to increase the circulation of their magazines and reviews. To arrive at their aim they are trying to get subscriptions to their publications in an indirect way. First of all, I must say I have no objection at all to the publication of those reviews, but I do object to their method of getting subscriptions.
There has been a decision in the courts, in the province of Quebec, to the effect that a contract cannot be a unilateral proposition. Therefore, if someone is receiving reviews, magazines or newspapers without having subscribed to them there is a way out. It is to refuse the publication, and send it back. In the province of Quebec no publisher can collect money from an individual who does not sign an agreement to receive a publication for a year, a month or two years. Of course, from another point of view I recognize that publishers are abusing their rights and are trying by all means to increase, if not their circulation, the amount of subscriptions. I am against that method of getting magazines into this country. I am against all kinds of pressure. I am not going to blame the department of the Postmaster General. The

department has nothing to do with this problem. It is not the duty of the department to open the letters of publishers to see what is in them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has just said that the Post Office Department has nothing to do with the problem he is discussing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He had better withdraw that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I should advise the hon. member that I brought a similar point to the attention of the hon. member for Vancouver East, who then related his remarks to the Post Office Department. I would ask the hon. member who has the floor to bring his remarks within the discussion of the administration of the Post Office Department.

I was coming to that. I was saying that the department has no responsibility for that method of carrying on business. If the department could find a way to overcome the difficulty that now confronts the people of Canada with respect to these magazines I would ask it to do so. I think they could overcome the present situation by getting in touch with the department of the postmaster general in the United States and making representations to this effect. We must be free to subscribe to publications of any kind, provided that the morality of the same is safeguarded. I have nothing to say against them. The only departments which can help the people of Canada resist the pressure campaigns of publishers of all sorts of magazines in this country are the departments of the Postmaster General of Canada and of the United States.

I suppose that no department of government enters into the daily life of every Canadian citizen as much as does the postal department. When I say that, I should like to pay my tribute to the parliamentary assistant, who is so ably carrying on the duties of the Postmaster General, who is ill.
The remarks I have to make tonight will be brief. There are two or three matters that are of particular interest to Canadians. The first is this. In a world that has been speeded up in the last 25 years the post office has not kept pace with the speedy developments. I see the parliamentary assistant looking at me and probably thinking of airmail. Twenty-five years ago a letter posted in London before five or six o'clock in the afternoon would be delivered in Toronto the next morning. Two months ago a friend of mine posted a letter in London and two days later it was delivered in Toronto. At the

same place at the same time he posted a special delivery letter, and it was delivered three days later in Toronto. It was addressed by the same man to the same persons and posted on the same day at the same post office.
When the all-up airmail was introduced, most Canadians thought they were going to get speedy mail delivery, but such is not the case. Thousands and thousands of Canadians who are paying a 25 per cent increase in first class mail rates, which is what the increase amounted to a year ago, are not getting any advantage from all-up airmail because of the fact that they do not live in areas where airmail is available. Much of the airmail within the province never gets to a plane at all. It is only when large distances are to be traversed that the all-up mail really comes into effect. An editorial in the St. Thomas Times-Journal of March 17, 1954, had this to say:
People In the big cities may benefit from the all-air mail service, but the vast majority of Canadians who live in rural districts or in centres remote from airports used by T.C.A. will suffer grave inconvenience. There is real merit in the suggestion that a special stamp be issued that would serve as an ironclad guarantee that mail when desired shall move only by rail.
That indicates the thinking of some people in the country. I have here a news item which appeared in the London Free Press protesting the slash in the rail service in western Canada. It states:
Changes in the Stratford-Sarnia route become effective next Monday.
It was also announced that a truck will take over from the train in carrying mail between Sarnia and Stratford.
It goes on to point out that a passenger unit will leave Sarnia Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday morning at 8.30 beginning March 14. The train will make the return trip from Stratford Monday, Wednesday and Friday. I might mention this news item was written a year ago. If they have to depend on a schedule like that the people in that area are going to have a much poorer mail service than they have now. There is no provision in these trucks for sorting mail en route, which means that in many cases mail will have to be rerouted over the same route a couple of days later.
The establishment of the 40-hour week has made the people employed in the railway mail services begin to think that they are the forgotten people. Because of particular routes and train schedules they are penalized.
The United States has introduced a diesel motor truck which is equipped in the same way as the railway mail car. In many cases
Supply-Post Office
this service has proved to be more efficient and cheaper than the rail service. We are facing a problem as far as railroad revenues are concerned, especially in the case of the Canadian National Railways, and therefore I submit that motor truck routes should be set up only in those cases where the railways do not give a service.
There are four or five such routes that could be established in the vicinity of London, and I would just mention Clinton, Wingham, Kincardine, Wiarton and the Stratford-Sarnia service to which I referred a moment ago. I think western Ontario would provide a good area for an experiment of this nature because of the density of population, the conditions of the highways and the fact that there is a central administration point at London which is equidistant between Windsor and Toronto and serving the northern area of Huron and Bruce.
For the information of the minister I will send over this copy of the National Geographic magazine of July, 1954, which describes the development of this motor truck service where the sorting is done en route. In the truck service provided in Ontario no sorting is done en route. By adopting this other method the sorting could be done en route and mail delivery made much sooner than it is now.

I should like to endorse what the previous speaker has said, that while an excellent airmail service is provided for the larger towns some of the smaller towns are not getting the type of service they deserve, and I refer particularly to the interior of British Columbia. I suggest that the minister start to make greater use of the small air lines operating between Calgary and Penticton, and Vancouver and Penticton. This would speed up the service in that area.
What I rose particularly to do was to pass on several complaints I have received from British Columbia with reference to the period between the calling of tenders and the expiry date for filing applications for the conveyance of mail between stations and post offices and so on. I submit that an extra week's time should be given before the final date of acceptance, this to apply west of Winnipeg and definitely throughout British Columbia.
The nature of the complaints varies. One complaint I have is that the notice appeared in the post office for just one day before it was taken down. The person complaining did not know who had taken it down. Another complaint is that the notice was taken down

Supply-Post Office
the same day it was put up. Presumably someone interested in the contract did not want any competition.
I suggest that there be a penalty for anyone removing such a poster from a post office before the time has expired for the receiving of tenders. I can give the minister the particulars of these complaints if he wishes to have them, but I understand that they are fairly general. Members of parliament receive copies of these notices but in many cases there is no possible chance of sending them along to someone in British Columbia who might be interested in tendering but could not get a tender in on time owing to the short period allowed for that purpose.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Vancouver East referred to the mails being used for the disposal of merchandise. X wish to warn the Postmaster General that when door to door service in place of a box service is introduced he might be on the lookout for people who send out little metal mail boxes. You wonder where it comes from, but after a while you get a letter saying it is worth $2.75. When you write back and say that you do not want the thing they ask you to pay the return postage. I suggest to the Acting Postmaster General that he note this, because it will happen again.

Mr. Chairman, last year when the Postmaster General introduced a bill to change the postal rates we had the benefit of a report which had been issued on March 1,
1953.	This year we did not have the benefit of the report of the department for some reason or another. I am not criticizing them for that fact. The report is dated October 1,
1954,	and for the report that I have here I am indebted to the parliamentary assistant who allowed me to have it so that I could make some kind of comparison between last year's report and this year's report.
When they introduced the increased postal rates last year they anticipated a deficit in the department of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $13,500,000. I just thought that I would check over those figures with the report this year, and I find that they just do not seem to stand up. That brings back the contention that we made last year that there was not any justification for increasing the rates until such time as the suggested changes that were to be made in the department were put into effect, as recommended by J. D. Woods and Gordon and that then we would see what the outcome would be. But the department maintained that nevertheless the

increased rate had to go into operation if the department was even going to carry itself for the next year.
Here is what they estimated. I will quote from last year's Hansard of January 14, 1954, at page 1124 when I quoted the Postmaster General's contention:
. . . as I followed the reasons for the increase in the postal rates advanced by the Postmaster General, they are the five-day week or the forty-hour week at a cost of $5 million; the increase in wages that is involved in the amount of $7 million, and for the rural mail $1,500,000, amounting to approximately $13,500,000.
Then on top of that they estimated a deficit in the department, for the withdrawal of the excise revenue tax, of another $7 million or $7,500,000. It was a very extensive figure that ran into anywhere from $13 million to $20 million.
Our position in the opposition was this. We did not find out, until it was mentioned on the bottom of the page in the introduction, that they had received valuable assistance from the firm of J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited, management consultants. We wanted to know what that was all about. It was not for some considerable time afterwards that we were given the opportunity to look at the report and its contents were very revealing. The suggestions, recommendations or observations in it, if they had been followed out, would have made considerable economies in that department. In view of the report itself that had been tendered last year, the Postmaster General's report and the J. D. Woods and Gordon report, it would have been only fair to the people of this country if the government had introduced these changes before imposing the additional rates. That is what I should like to cover tonight.
There has been some improvement in the operation of the department. It is all very well when we criticize them for what we think is not competent or efficient operation. But when there has been improvement in the department they are at least entitled to some commendation, and there has been considerable improvement.
But I should just like to take their own figures. I quoted last year that over a period of 20 years there has been an increase every year in the revenue of some $4 million and that there has likewise been an increase in the expenditures, but on the sum total there has been a surplus or a profit each year; and I pointed out what had been done in the past by the postmaster general, the one outstanding postmaster general since confederation, Sir William Mulock. When he had charge of the department it was more or less his ambition and his goal to make it

work and to make it pay. He surprised everybody in that day by what he did. Instead of increasing rates, as soon as postal volume increased he would reduce rates. Then there would be a deficit for a year or so. Then following that, revenue would pick up in the course of three or four years and he would again have a surplus. He kept on doing this and he was criticized for it.
But the picture has changed. Now we have the postmasters general increasing rates and they have increased the rates. Inside of 10 years they have increased them by 100 per cent. Now they have increased revenue, but in this report it is not shown that there is increased revenue because the rates did not go into effect last year until April 1, 1954. The figures we have in the 1954 report of this department are based on the old rates of last year, with the one exception, namely the withdrawal of the excise revenue from cheques.
If you examine the figures closely and with the increase in wages that has taken place, you will find that the figures work out nearly to a balance or even-Stephen. He estimated the deficit on the excise revenue from cheques at about $5 million. It turned out to be some $7,500,000. He estimated the increase in wages at about $5 million for rural mail carriers, and other carriers at about $1,500,000. It did not work out to that because on their own figures of expenditures, in this report for 1954, on page 14-when you get the report you can look it up-there is shown an increase for salaries and allowances paid to revenue post offices, some staff post offices and sub-post offices. It amounts to a total of, in 1952-53, $15,417,000. For the year 1953-54 it is $16,636,000 or an increase of approximately $1,120,000. There is a vast difference between what the minister suggested was going to take place in the department because they are working exactly as they were last year, on the same set-up, with the exception, as I pointed out, of the withdrawal of the revenue from the excise stamps on cheques. But I pointed this out last year to them when we were discussing it, after we had the benefit of the J. D. Woods and Gordon report. Last year the Postmaster General, when he was supplementing his remarks, said:
Perhaps I may complete my views on that subject. We had a surplus last year of $61 million and this year we are going to have a deficit of $1 million. This deficit will result through the loss of $71 million by the cancellation of the excise tax.
He says there will be a $5 million deficit due to the adoption of the 40-hour week, and $7 million due to the increase in wages of
Supply-Post Office
the general post office staff, $1,500,000 due to the increase to rural mail carriers and approximately $1 million covers the increase to the railway company, all this dealing in the realm of conjecture. I go on further to point out that the addition to the post office revenue that the minister was asking from the excise stamps on cheques was unwarranted, for this tax had its proper place in the consolidated revenue fund. To suggest the inclusion of receipts from this tax in the Post Office Department service or deficit was entirely wrong. In the first place the only conclusion that can be drawn is that it was an indirect way of supplying funds that were necessary for subsidies and subventions within the department.
It is now apparent that these concealed subsidies will have to be paid from the consolidated revenue fund and not from postal revenues. That is about what will take place. With the withdrawal of the $7 million benefit from their operations it just about brings the department out even. Next year when the increased rates will be in effect there will be a surplus of something like $14 million on the estimate of the Postmaster General, and I think the people of the country will feel that they have been taken in.
I mentioned last year that there were some illustrations of stamps in the report of the department. There was one very beautiful stamp. I guess you would call it a picture of a blue goose. At that time I think I described it as the goose that laid the golden egg for the government and said that if they were not very careful and if they pressed their luck too far they would kill the goose that laid the golden egg. This year in their report they have a new series of stamps which are also very good. One appears to be a polar bear, I presume, with the aurora borealis behind it. Then there is one of a mountain goat. There is also one of a reindeer or elk. I think it would be worth while if they had one with a fish, a clammy looking big sucker, to portray exactly what the government is doing to the people of Canada. They are just playing them for suckers with the increased postage rates and it would be very appropriate if they would introduce such a stamp to let the people know what is happening to them.
I have been checking over the changes in the department in the light of the recommendations in the Woods and Gordon report from the point of view of the economies that could be effected. Certain changes in the staff were recommended. I think I put on record last year a number of the changes and recommendations contained in the report which if followed out would bring about

Supply-Post Office
economies in the operation of the department. They have carried out some of them. I have been comparing the organization of the Post Office Department this year with last year. They have been introducing changes, and I think it is all for the best that they are doing so.
Last year there were some 30 personnel divisions; they have made a rearrangement. There are some six branches this year and 38 personnel divisions, an increase of one branch and eight personnel divisions to operate the department in line with the recommendations of the Woods and Gordon report. We will not be able to get a real picture of the situation until next year because we do not know what is the full effect on the revenues with the increased postage rates. That is not apparent in the report for the year ended April, 1954 compared with the one ended April, 1953, and the rates have not been in effect for a full year. I have not had sufficient time to compare the 1954 report but offhand I would say that the revenues do not bear out the contention made by the Postmaster General that there would be a deficit. On their own figures they wiped out a surplus of $6 million odd last year, and for this year I think the amount is around $2,474,000, but they have not had a chance to get the benefit of the increased revenues for a full year. If you compare the financial results for the past 20 years, the result still comes out the same as it did last year. There were only three years in those 20 years in which there was a deficit. In all those years the surplus averaged about $100,000.
In face of that I suggest the department should consider reducing the postage rates again because, even on the figures they gave us, their contention has not been upheld. When they have the benefit of the increased rates for a full year they are going to have a surplus, and I do not know what their story is going to be then. It was contended that with the introduction of the 40-hour week for postal employees and the increased wages for postal employees and the rural mail carriers there would be a deficit of somewhere around $12 million, but all that shows up in this year's report is $1,250,000.
The estimating of the department is very much out, and if that is the kind of estimating they are capable of the house should not have very much faith in their estimates for the future on the basis of this performance. Mention is made of improvement of the postal service and the question of public relations from the point of view of educating people to address their mail properly with the right
[Mr. Small.l
name and address so as to help the postal carrier. I suppose one cannot be too critical of that, but there is some cause for humour in it. In the old days when someone had moved or there had been some changes or there were misdirections or wrong numbers on letters you could always rely on the postman on the beat. He would see that letters got to the right place without too much difficulty. He would say that so and so had moved up the street or over to the next street and he would make the correction himself.
I have had mail sent back to me when there was only a difference in the address of six or seven houses from the place where the person had moved. These letters have come back with the notation, "Not known, not at this address." Yet the individual was living on the same street only five or six doors removed from his old address. One might say that there was a new man on the beat but still that does not warrant it because the people living at the old address will tell the postman that the former resident has only moved three or four doors away. But the postal carriers now must have instructions from the department to return the letter to the post office if the people are not at the address, and letters are returned irrespective of the expense involved.
I do not say this by way of criticism of the heads of the department, but I do say it is a change from the good old days when you could rely on the postman to see that the mail got to the right place. I would ask that next year we receive the report of the department in time for us to make comparisons. Then we would be in a better position to offer constructive criticism of the operations of the department. At the present time we are more or less just taking a guess at what has happened. I was fortunate, as I said, in that the parliamentary assistant let me have his copy of the report so I could make a hasty summary of it. If my remarks do not jibe entirely with the report it is because I have summarized it in haste, and when I have a chance to go over it more thoroughly I will probably have something further to say.

Mr. Chairman, I am not at all sure that the little bouquet I had for the minister may not have one or two skunk cabbage leaves in it too as in the case of the member who has just spoken. He remarked that he had noticed some improvements in the Post Office Department in the last year, and I was rather hesitant about rising right after him because I was afraid that the shock of two opposition members making remarks of that nature one after the other

415S
might be too great for the minister to stand. However, I shall say at once my remarks are going to be somewhat more brief than perhaps they were on this item a year ago. At that time I had occasion to remind the Postmaster General of a statement which had been made that when the new postal rates went into effect all first class mail would be carried by air wherever such carriage would speed its delivery. I said at that time I hoped to discover the Postmaster General would realize that Canada did not stop at Vancouver. I am very glad to be able to state this year that so far as I am concerned some recognition has been given to that fact, and there has been some improvement made in the matter of the carriage of mail by air to some of the more remote places in British Columbia.
I hope that having said that the minister and his officials will not simply sit back and bask in those remarks. I hope they will recognize that in a good many respects there is still some room for improvement in that situation. I could, of course, go on to tell them of the fact that there are at least two places where we badly need new post office buildings and other places where better facilities are needed. However, I shall not take the time to go into all the details of that tonight.
I was interested in some remarks which were made this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant. I was not quite able to follow all of' them, but they concerned the possibility of improved conditions, and in some cases improved income, for the postmasters in revenue post offices. I hope that the result of his remarks is that there will be a further improvement in that particular direction. I do know that in many cases in communities where, on a straight revenue basis, the post office may not appear to be very important, nevertheless the duties which are being performed year in and year out by these postmasters are certainly far beyond the scale of remuneration they have been receiving. I believe there is an area of the public service which, in a great many cases, could very well receive better financial recognition than has been the case.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer), who spoke this afternoon on the estimates of the Post Office Department, I want to offer to the minister, who has been away from the house for quite some time owing to ill health, my best wishes for a quick and complete recovery. I am sure that all hon. members have regretted his absence and missed his smile and good humour.
Supply-Post Office
The sympathetic Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) has been compelled for several years to work hard under unfavourable conditions, not to say unbearable.
We often find that in certain branches of the department, the minister only plays a secondary part and that he is, as it were, a front that must be saved. The Postmaster General is one of those ministers whose authority exists in name only and who is not permitted to play the part assigned to him.
That is not as good as the first part.

Wait until the end.
He must nevertheless face our bitter criticisms on the administration of the department and cover as best he can those who have given orders one way or the other and who are the real masters and authorities in the department.
We are particularly concerned with this today. No one can deny that the great master of the situation, the one who makes and cancels decisions, the one who rules the roost within the department, in the presence or in the absence of the minister, is none other than the all-powerful deputy minister, Mr. Walter Turnbull.
Listen!

Far be it from me to think that the minister-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order; the Acting Postmaster General having raised this matter as a point of order, I suppose it is my responsibility to settle it to the extent that it can be settled. I would say that criticism of the Postmaster General, even in his absence, in his capacity as Postmaster General is undoubtedly in order. The administration of the department is before the committee at this stage and it is the only stage in our proceedings during which the administration of the department can be criticized. Criticism of the administration of the department is the privilege of the members of the house.
I do not believe it is the duty or the responsibility of the chairman of the committee to try to guide members in what is or is not ethical or in good tastt, I should like to express my personal opinion that the conduct of the department is a fair subject for criticism even though, through unfortunate circumstances, the minister is absent. I might perhaps be permitted to go this much farther and to suggest to members that criticism of a nature which could only be answered personally by the minister himself and which, under the force of circumstances, could not be answered either by the acting minister or the parliamentary assistant, might safely be left unsaid at this time. I do not think I have the power or the right to go farther than that.

Mr. Chairman, thus far I have not criticized at all the Postmaster

General, and it is not my intention to do so. A few moments ago I was speaking in French, and I shall continue to do so.
(Translation) :
Mr. Chairman, far be it from me to think that the minister is not qualified to conduct the affairs of his department were he given the opportunity to do it, but in the case of the present minister as well as in the case of those who preceded him in this position since the end of the last war, history repeats itself.
In this connection, I wish to quote from an editorial by Mr. Pierre Chaloult which appeared in the Ottawa paper he Droit on April 19, 1955, under the heading:
The Battle Against Shadows
We hear about the impending resignation of one of the youngest and most active members of the federal cabinet. Mr. Alcide Cote, who, as the rumour goes, would no longer be able to work twelve hours a day, the time needed to supervise the administrative mafia entrenched in the Post Office Department for some years.
In other words, the report has it that they finally wore down this incumbent as they did his immediate predecessors.
For it is obvious that the Post Office Department, formerly a realm of peace and quiet, can only be thought of now in terms of insoluble problems, while the ministers, one after the other, not only come to their wits' end but lose face, however strong they may be physically and politically.
When, indeed, Mr. Ernest Bertrand, on August 29, 1945, left the Department of Fisheries to become Postmaster General, he found, when he assumed his duties, a new deputy minister, Mr. Walter James Turnbull.
The latter knew the department inside out. He had spent his career there before becoming private secretary to the then prime minister who had just made him a deputy minister, no doubt as a reward for services rendered.
Now, it so happens that from that time on, exactly, the history of that department has ceased to be that of the minister in charge of that portfolio to become that of the deputy minister whose hand has never ceased to appear in every intrigue, every plot, every difficulty which has beset the representatives of the department in the federal cabinet.
After three and a half years of undistinguished rule, Mr. Bertrand abandoned politics as well as his portfolio which he passed on to one of the most brilliant and dynamic representatives of the rising generation, Mr. Edouard Rinfret who, following a short though hectic stay in that position, was obliged, in turn, to bow to Mr. Turnbull, until such time as Mr. Alcide Cote will be compelled to do likewise.
Such an opposition, hidden but unmistakable, between the deputy minister and the minister was in no manner helpful to the latter and, both under the administration of Mr. Rinfret and that of Mr. Cote, there were debates during which the postmaster general, hedged in all around, had to fight off not only the three opposition parties, which is normal, but also his own administration (which is less normal) and even some of his colleagues who under the pretence of help threw banana peels under his feet. In other words, blows came not only from the front and from below but also from behind.

Such tactics were evidently not of the kind to help the minister consolidate his position, and the deputy minister, back in the shadows, could gloat with pleasure and lick his chops, which he evidently did.
What would Mr. Turnbull be hoping for besides his present position? Why is he so bold as to risk everything, including a false step which might bring about his downfall?
What purpose was he following in all these intrigues? Could it be that, as former secretary to Mr. Mackenzie King, as was, from 1924 to 1926, Mr. Ralph Campney (now Minister of National Defence), as was from 1937 to 1952 Mr. John Pickersgill (now Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, as well as acting Postmaster General), as was Mr. Lester Pearson, former deputy minister of the former prime minister himself (now Secretary of State, that is, minister, for External Affairs), just as his former colleagues who lived within the orbit of the former master, Mr. Turnbull was hoping to see himself some day appointed Postmaster General?
What poppycock!

Maybe the relations between the minister and his deputy minister would then become less intricate?
Who knows!
This article, in my opinion, gives the perfect picture of the situation that had obtained for a long time within the Post Office Department, a situation for which, as you will note, the present deputy minister, Mr. Turnbull, is solely responsible. This situation being generally known, it is, doubtless, one of the main reasons for which we sympathize so much with the Postmaster General.
There is confusion in the post office administration, a confusion that was evidenced last year by my hon. friend from Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton) and admitted by the hon. minister, because the authority responsible for the department is not respected. It has been replaced by that of the deputy minister, who is in no way answerable to either the people or parliament.
Most of the time unaware of what is going on, the minister is caught in an unqualifiable position, facing a cross-fire of protests from all sides. Unfortunately, his job ends there, except for a few speeches now and then, at the opening of a new post office, or when he has to represent the Prime Minister at some place when the latter is unable to attend because of his numerous engagements. Now is the time more than ever to have the ministers administer their own departments and not inferiors who get their bureaucratic authority from I do not know where. If the deputy minister, as in the case of Mr. Turnbull, takes over certain powers which belong only to the minister, who is solely responsible to the people and to parliament, a superior authority, in this instance the Prime
Supply-Post Office
Minister, should put an end to this unseemly monopolizing which is a serious obstacle to a good administration.
Having set forth this extremely important principle, I will now come to another problem which deserves the full attention of the department, of the house and the whole population.
On February 24 last, the hon. Minister of Labour told the house that an employment agency which claimed to find jobs within the organization which is to build the St. Lawrence seaway had been precluded from using the mail. And the minister added that other similar companies were being investigated.
I was one of the first to endorse these steps to protect our working public against some exploiters. The agency was ordered to explain its action within 10 days before a hearing committee of the department. We have never been told what was the outcome of the inquiry, but we know that the mail service was suspended at that time for this agency until it would prove that it was not guilty of the charge laid against it of having used Her Majesty's mail to make false representations. Such procedure meant that the local office no longer delivered mail to the agency and that letters were returned to senders.
All honest people were glad of that decision and the Post Office Department was congratulated for the energetic stand it had taken.
That wonderful picture is marred, however, Mr. Chairman, by circumstances which bring forth the conflicting attitudes of the Post Office Department and of the federal government.
At the very moment when an agency fraudulently obtaining money from the people is prevented from using the postal services, which is excellent, the propagandists of that infamous ideology known as communism are still allowed to distribute their pernicious literature in all Canadian homes. This infernal propaganda, however, does not merely aim at subtracting a few hard-earned dollars from the taxpayers, but its self-imposed devilish mission is first to poison and then to kill the soul and heart of all those candidly trustful people, who yield to this indoctrination. The hon. members of this house are not spared by this communist literature and are snowed under by letters and publications arriving by mail at their offices, even without postage on them.

As a citizen of the province of Quebec more particularly I cannot let the sickle and the hammer become the symbol of honour.
I would like to draw the attention of the Postmaster General to a certain bureaucracy, not to say gestapo, which is now prevailing in his department in the city of Quebec. I believe that the minister has realized what is happening, because I am told two officials from the department in Ottawa, Messrs. Craig and Charlebois, are now in Quebec to investigate the matter and find out what is going on.
The employees are said to be complaining of the harsh treatment. In fact those who could be doing their work sitting down are no longer allowed to use a seat. An iron rule prevails there. The government has undoubtedly become aware of it because I am told two investigators are now making a thorough investigation into the dictatorial doings of certain officials.
If, in the course of this investigation, present employees are interviewed, I would suggest to the department that all those who, within the last year for example, have either been dismissed or have resigned for the simple reason that, in their judgment, they were working in an unbearable atmosphere, be also consulted so that we may know the real reasons behind either their resignations or their dismissal.
I will also bring to the attention of the acting minister a refusal which cannot be justified and that I had to put up with some time ago when I asked for some information which should be available to any member of parliament, as it did not call for the production of any confidential documents.
I wanted to know, once, in order to compile some statistics on employment, what was the amount of unemployment insurance stamps which had been bought at the post office and distributed in the district. I was flatly denied this information, on the grounds that an order from the minister was necessary to divulge this information.
Some departmental officials are usurping privileges which should normally be denied them. I believe that elected representatives of the people are entitled to this information, particularly in view of the fact that it becomes public knowledge overnight.
I protest against this state of affairs and I hope that the minister will see to it that this does not happen again.
I now have another suggestion to offer the Post Office Department. For a number of years, the Quebec Power Company, of Quebec

city, had a contract with the department allowing mail carriers and certain other classes of postal employees to travel free on Quebec city buses-or street cars at the time. Numerous representations have been made on behalf of the mail carriers since the day the company decided against renewing this contract. However, the department would only consent to allow its mail carriers two street car tickets per day. This, to my mind, is unfair, considering the privileges they previously enjoyed. There have been talks between the departmental officials and the Quebec Power Company, but, so far, to no avail.
I am not trying to blame the department for that failure, since I am told that it was the company that refused to grant that privilege to the postal employees. The new agreement between the company and the city of Quebec withdraws that privilege from policemen and firemen as well as from letter carriers.
I know for a fact however that the Post Office Department has offered to pay the Quebec Power Company $113.33 a year per letter carrier for their transportation, and that the company refused the offer. These poor employees are now receiving only two tickets a day and must pay out of their own pocket the additional tickets they need to reach their place of work, get their mail and deliver it.
Let me point out that the offer of the department to the Quebec Power Company is fair and that every letter carrier is entitled to that amount.
Raising the mail carrier's wages by $113.33, which is the amount offered to the Quebec Power, would give all concerned a square deal. If the employee spends only from $50 to $60 a year, the difference would be his to keep. If, on the contrary, he travels by bus often enough to spend more than $113.33, let him pay it out of his own pocket. I feel that would be an act of elementary justice for those devoted public servants who never miss an opportunity to serve the people.
I already had an opportunity, some time ago, to convey to this house a suggestion made to me by the various credit unions throughout Canada which now have a membership of 1,500,000, of whom 1 million are in the province of Quebec.
Requests reached me from all the credit unions in the city and district of Quebec, asking me to speak on their behalf to the minister in order that, during 1955, the birth

of their founder, a man who did so much good for the people, especially in the homes of working people, be commemorated by the issue of a postage stamp bearing the effigy of that great Canadian. The request is as follows:
Whereas the Post Office Department issues from time to time postage stamps bearing the effigy of prominent people who have been illustrious in Canadian life:
Whereas Commander Alphonse Desjardins was the founder of the credit unions;
Whereas his work has now spread to all parts of Canada and in the two Americas, and renders immeasurable services;
Whereas the year 1955 marks the centenary of the birth of Mr. Desjardins;
Whereas the founder of credit unions is recognized as a Canadian benefactor;
Be it resolved:
That the board of directors of the credit union, representing a certain number of members . . .
I am not going to mention any particular group, because there are a great many of them.
. . . express the wish that a stamp be issued in honour of Commander Desjardins, and that a copy of this resolution be addressed to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, the Hon. Alcide Cote, the Hon. Cyrille Vaillancourt, the Hon. Chas. G. Power, and Mr. Wilfrid Dufresne, M.P.
All his life, that great Canadian dedicated himself by teaching thrift, and I think the Postmaster General should seize the occasion of the centenary of Commander Desjardins' birth to pay him a tribute by issuing, in 1955, a stamp bearing his effigy.
Mr. Chairman, we are told that a new post office will shortly be built in Quebec city on a block of land registered until lately by the city of Quebec, but the registration of which was recently cancelled to enable the federal government to purchase the land.
A letter was sent a short time ago to all store owners and to all people who have homes within that block, ordering them to leave the premises on May 31, if they did not want to become liable to the penalties provided by law. The said letter was sent on May 6 last, which means that those merchants who have been in business at that same place for the past 50 years, were given only three weeks to get out.
In the name of all those people who would be only too glad to move elsewhere, provided they be given sufficient time, I urge the Post Office Department authorities to speak on their behalf to the Department of Public Works so that this post office may not be erected right now and so that they be given time to find new locations. In Quebec, as elsewhere, there is a housing problem; people living in those houses should be given time to find another home.

And what about unemployment of which the hon. member speaks so much?

I was expecting that question from the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert). He wants to speak about unemployment? A post office is to be erected. I did not object to the construction of that building but I believe that it should be built in a more suitable place.
To begin with, I do not know whether the Quebec municipal council has been stampeded into this, but this registration must have been sanctioned yesterday in the superior court. And yet it had provided for the demolition, at a given time, of all the buildings in this block in order to improve traffic conditions in Quebec city.
The distinguished French town planner, Jacques Greber, was among those who had submitted recommendations to the town planning committee. I cannot understand how it is that the Post Office Department can so summarily dismiss the views expressed by Mr. Greber and make such short shrift of a plan prepared by competent authorities. Why does it have to erect, in the very heart of the city, where traffic moves only very slowly as it is, a building far exceeding in area the block of which I spoke, in such a way as to prevent any easing in cross-town traffic conditions.
May I be permitted to tell the minister that at that spot, traffic congestion is frequent and that about 133,000 vehicles pass that point between eight o'clock in the morning and eight o'clock at night. The streets of Quebec city are already narrow enough and I do not see why the federal government would wish to add to the traffic problem and would want to build a post office-
